about: Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism (MBBS0016) is described in UCL's 2026/27 module catalogue as the fourth of four modules taken in MBBS Year 1. It is taught in person in Terms 2 and 3 (in the May 2026 version of the 2026–27 timetable, mainly from mid-February to late March 2027, with a further block at the end of April) and carries 0 credits. UCL's 2026/27 module catalogue says it combines basic science with common clinical problems of the kidney and gastrointestinal tract, metabolic imbalance, and fluid and electrolyte balance; covers the anatomy, histology, development and function of the gut and abdominal organs; looks at how diet supports health and prevents disease; and aims to build skills in interpreting images of internal organs and in calculating measures of nutritional status, renal function and acid–base balance. UCL does not publish a topic list or learning outcomes, so the topics here follow the order of that official description and aims. Year 1 knowledge is tested in the end-of-year Applied Knowledge Tests (online SBA and VSA papers). This pack is educational revision material, not clinical advice, and gives no drug or fluid doses, volumes or rates.

Digestion and absorption, and how the gut is controlled
Energy metabolism: fed, fasting and starvation
Body fluid compartments, osmolality and water balance
Sodium, potassium, volume control and IV fluid principles
The kidney: filtration, tubular function and kidney injury

notes.h: Gut and abdominal organ anatomy, histology and development
notes.overview: The abdomen holds the gut tube, its accessory organs and their blood supply, arranged around the peritoneum. This topic covers the layered gut wall, which organs are intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal, the foregut, midgut and hindgut pattern of blood supply and development, and how plain films, ultrasound and CT show these structures.
objectives: Describe the four layers of the gut wall and where the enteric plexuses lie.
Distinguish intraperitoneal from retroperitoneal organs.
Match foregut, midgut and hindgut to their artery, embryological origin and referred pain.
Explain why absorbed nutrients and drugs reach the liver first.
Apply a simple system to a plain abdominal radiograph (bowel calibre, gas, free air, calcification).

sections.h: The gut tube and its wall
sections.body:
The alimentary canal (gut) runs from mouth to anus; accessory organs (salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas) pour secretions into it through ducts. From the lumen outwards the wall has four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa and serosa (the oesophagus has an outer adventitia instead of serosa).
- Mucosa: epithelium, lamina propria and a thin muscularis mucosae. The epithelium matches the job: stratified squamous (non-keratinised) in the oesophagus to resist abrasion, simple columnar in the stomach and intestines for secretion and absorption.
- Submucosa: connective tissue with vessels, lymphatics and the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, which controls local secretion. Duodenal submucosa contains Brunner's glands that secrete alkaline mucus.
- Muscularis externa: inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle with the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus between them, which controls motility.
- Serosa: the visceral peritoneum.
The small intestine is built for absorption. Circular folds, villi and microvilli (the brush border) give a surface area of roughly 200 m² (approximate), and each villus contains a lacteal that takes up absorbed fat. Peyer's patches (lymphoid tissue) are a feature of the ileum. The large intestine has no villi but many mucus-secreting goblet cells.

The parietal peritoneum lines the abdominal wall and the visceral peritoneum covers the organs. Organs hung on a mesentery (jejunum, ileum, transverse and sigmoid colon) are intraperitoneal and mobile; the duodenum (mostly), pancreas, ascending and descending colon and rectum are retroperitoneal, lying behind the peritoneum.
The gut tube develops in three parts, each with its own artery and its own pattern of referred pain (vertebral levels approximate):
- Foregut (oesophagus to the second part of the duodenum, plus liver, gallbladder and pancreas): coeliac trunk (about T12); pain felt in the epigastrium.
- Midgut (rest of the duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon): superior mesenteric artery (about L1); pain felt around the umbilicus.
- Hindgut (distal third of the transverse colon to the upper anal canal): inferior mesenteric artery (about L3); pain felt in the suprapubic region.
Venous blood from the gut drains through the hepatic portal vein to the liver before reaching the heart, so absorbed nutrients, drugs and toxins meet the liver first.
In development the midgut grows faster than the abdominal cavity, herniates into the umbilical cord and returns while rotating about 270° anticlockwise (viewed from the front) around the superior mesenteric artery. Malrotation predisposes to volvulus, a twist of bowel that can cut off its blood supply. A persistent remnant of the vitelline duct forms Meckel's diverticulum, classically described by the 'rule of 2s' (about 2% of people, roughly 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve; approximate).

Plain abdominal radiograph. It shows gas patterns, some calcification and soft-tissue outlines, but gives a poor view of structures at the back of the abdomen. Use a system.
- Bowel calibre (the '3/6/9 rule'): small bowel up to about 3 cm, colon up to about 6 cm, caecum up to about 9 cm; larger suggests dilatation.
- Small-bowel valvulae conniventes cross the full width of the lumen and tend to lie centrally; large-bowel haustra usually do not cross it and the colon lies around the periphery. The distinction is helpful but not completely reliable.
- Calcified gallstones (right upper quadrant) and renal stones may be seen.
- Free gas from a perforation is best shown as gas under the diaphragm on an erect chest radiograph; Rigler's sign (gas on both sides of the bowel wall) is a plain-film clue.
Ultrasound uses no ionising radiation and is good for the gallbladder and bile ducts, the kidneys and free fluid, but bowel gas and body habitus limit it. CT shows all the abdominal organs in cross-section and is used when more detail is needed, at the cost of a higher radiation dose.

A 72-year-old with previous abdominal surgery has colicky central abdominal pain, vomiting and distension and has passed no wind. The abdominal radiograph shows centrally placed dilated loops up to 4.5 cm wide, with folds crossing the whole lumen, and little gas in the colon. Small-bowel obstruction is likely, and adhesions are a common cause. The pain is central because the midgut refers to the umbilical region.
Vomiting and fluid collecting in the obstructed bowel make fluid and electrolyte balance an immediate concern, which links this topic to the rest of the module.

- Students often think every abdominal organ sits inside the peritoneal cavity. In fact the duodenum (mostly), pancreas, ascending and descending colon and rectum are retroperitoneal, which is why pancreatic pain can radiate to the back and why free gas may be absent after a retroperitoneal perforation.
- Students often think the portal vein carries blood straight to the heart. It carries gut blood to the liver first, so nutrients and drugs undergo hepatic processing (first-pass metabolism) before reaching the systemic circulation.
- Students often think foregut, midgut and hindgut are only positions. They are embryological divisions that determine arterial supply, nerve supply and where pain is felt.
- Students often think the colon is identified by position alone. Calibre, haustra and position together help, and no single sign is fully reliable.

notes.h: Digestion and absorption, and how the gut is controlled
notes.overview: Digestion is mechanical and chemical breakdown; absorption is uptake across the epithelium. This topic follows carbohydrate, protein and fat through the gut, shows where each is absorbed, and explains how nerves and hormones coordinate motility and secretion, with malabsorption as the clinical link.
objectives: List the six digestive activities and distinguish peristalsis from segmentation.
Explain how gastrin, secretin and CCK link gut contents to secretion.
Describe digestion and absorption of carbohydrate, protein and fat, including the roles of bile salts, micelles and chylomicrons.
Explain why sodium-coupled glucose absorption underpins oral rehydration.
Predict deficiencies and stool changes from loss of a gut region or secretion.

sections.body:
The gut carries out six activities: ingestion, propulsion, mechanical digestion, chemical digestion, absorption and defecation. Peristalsis (waves of contraction and relaxation) propels contents; segmentation (local contractions of circular muscle, mainly in the small intestine) mixes them and exposes them to the epithelium.
Control is layered. The enteric nervous system (myenteric plexus for motility, submucosal plexus for secretion) can run local reflexes on its own; the autonomic nervous system and hormones modulate it, and parasympathetic (vagal) activity generally increases secretion and motility. Three hormones are central to this control:
- Gastrin (G cells of the stomach): stimulates acid secretion by parietal cells.
- Secretin (duodenum, released when acidic chyme arrives): stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice that neutralises the acid.
- Cholecystokinin, CCK (duodenum, released when fat and protein arrive): stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic juice and gallbladder contraction.
Gastric secretion is described in cephalic (sight, smell, thought of food), gastric (food in the stomach) and intestinal phases. Gastric juice has a pH of about 1.5–3.5. Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, chief cells make pepsinogen (activated to pepsin by acid), and a thick bicarbonate-rich mucus layer protects the lining.

sections.h: Digestion and absorption of each nutrient
sections.body:
Carbohydrate. Salivary and pancreatic amylase break starch into short chains; brush-border enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase and others) finish the job, leaving the monosaccharides glucose, galactose and fructose. Glucose and galactose enter enterocytes by sodium-coupled cotransport (SGLT1), driven by the low intracellular sodium that the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains, and leave by facilitated diffusion; fructose enters by facilitated diffusion.
Protein. Acid and pepsin start digestion in the stomach. Pancreatic proteases (secreted as inactive zymogens, with trypsinogen activated by the brush-border enzyme enteropeptidase) and brush-border peptidases produce amino acids, dipeptides and tripeptides, absorbed mainly in the duodenum and jejunum.
Fat. Bile salts emulsify fat into small droplets so pancreatic lipase can split triglycerides into free fatty acids and monoglycerides. Bile salts and lecithin gather these products into micelles, which carry them to the brush border; they diffuse in, are rebuilt into triglycerides and packaged into chylomicrons, which are too large for blood capillaries and leave through the lacteals into lymph. Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K travel in micelles.
Site matters. Most absorption occurs in the duodenum and jejunum. The terminal ileum takes up the vitamin B12–intrinsic factor complex and recycles bile salts. About 9 L of fluid enters the small intestine daily (about 2.3 L from food and drink, the rest from secretions); about 90% is absorbed there and most of the rest in the colon, leaving a small volume in the faeces.

Loss of any step produces a recognisable pattern.
- Coeliac disease: an immune reaction to gluten damages the villi (villous atrophy), cutting surface area; typical results are iron, folate or B12 deficiency, diarrhoea and weight loss.
- Lactase deficiency: undigested lactose is osmotically active and fermented by colonic bacteria, giving bloating, gas and watery diarrhoea.
- Pancreatic insufficiency (for example chronic pancreatitis): too little lipase causes steatorrhoea (pale, bulky, foul, floating stools) and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
- Terminal ileal disease or resection: vitamin B12 deficiency, and bile salt loss that can cause diarrhoea and fat malabsorption.
- Autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia): loss of parietal cells removes intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed even though the ileum is healthy.
- Secretory diarrhoea (for example cholera): large volumes of chloride-driven secretion; the sodium-coupled glucose transporter still works, which is why glucose-containing oral rehydration solutions are effective.

Tests follow the suspected defect.
- Blood tests: full blood count (anaemia, macrocytosis), ferritin, B12, folate, vitamin D and albumin show which nutrients are deficient.
- Coeliac disease: tissue transglutaminase antibodies are a first test and a small-bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy.
- Faecal tests: faecal elastase is low in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency; the appearance of steatorrhoea supports fat malabsorption.
- Breath tests can detect lactose malabsorption.
- Endoscopy and imaging show structural disease, such as strictures or inflammation in the terminal ileum.

A 28-year-old woman has had tiredness, loose pale stools and bloating for months. She is anaemic with a low ferritin and low folate. Villous atrophy on duodenal biopsy explains both the malabsorption and the pattern of deficiency: iron and folate are absorbed in the proximal small intestine, the very region that coeliac disease damages first.
Gastroenteritis in a child teaches the opposite lesson. Even when diarrhoea is severe, glucose and sodium in an oral rehydration solution are absorbed together by the same cotransporter and draw water with them, which is why this simple solution can replace losses.

- Students often think digestion happens mainly in the stomach. In fact most chemical digestion and nearly all absorption occur in the small intestine; the stomach starts protein digestion, stores and mixes.
- Students often think bile contains digestive enzymes. It does not: bile salts emulsify fat and form micelles, while the digesting enzyme, lipase, comes from the pancreas.
- Students often think all absorbed fat enters the blood capillaries. Long-chain fats leave as chylomicrons through lacteals into lymph and reach the blood via the thoracic duct.
- Students often think diarrhoea means the gut absorbs nothing. Sodium-coupled glucose uptake persists in many causes of diarrhoea, which is the basis of oral rehydration.
- Students often think vitamin B12 deficiency means a poor diet. It is usually malabsorption: lack of intrinsic factor or terminal ileal disease.

Processes and control
The gut carries out six activities: ingestion, propulsion, mechanical digestion, chemical digestion, absorption and defecation. Peristalsis (waves of contraction and relaxation) propels contents; segmentation (local contractions of circular muscle, mainly in the small intestine) mixes them and exposes them to the epithelium.
Control is layered. The enteric nervous system (myenteric plexus for motility, submucosal plexus for secretion) can run local reflexes on its own; the autonomic nervous system and hormones modulate it, and parasympathetic (vagal) activity generally increases secretion and motility. Three hormones are central to this control:
- Gastrin (G cells of the stomach): stimulates acid secretion by parietal cells.
- Secretin (duodenum, released when acidic chyme arrives): stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice that neutralises the acid.
- Cholecystokinin, CCK (duodenum, released when fat and protein arrive): stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic juice and gallbladder contraction.
Gastric secretion is described in cephalic (sight, smell, thought of food), gastric (food in the stomach) and intestinal phases. Gastric juice has a pH of about 1.5–3.5. Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, chief cells make pepsinogen (activated to pepsin by acid), and a thick bicarbonate-rich mucus layer protects the lining.

Carbohydrate. Salivary and pancreatic amylase break starch into short chains; brush-border enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase and others) finish the job, leaving the monosaccharides glucose, galactose and fructose. Protein. Acid and pepsin start digestion in the stomach. Fat. Bile salts emulsify fat into small droplets so pancreatic lipase can split triglycerides into free fatty acids and monoglycerides. Bile salts and lecithin gather these products into micelles, which carry them to the brush border; they diffuse in, are rebuilt into triglycerides and packaged into chylomicrons, which are too large for blood capillaries and leave through the lacteals into lymph. Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K travel in micelles.
Site matters. Most absorption occurs in the duodenum and jejunum. The terminal ileum takes up the vitamin B12–intrinsic factor complex and recycles bile salts. Loss of any step produces a recognisable pattern.
- Coeliac disease: an immune reaction to gluten damages the villi (villous atrophy), cutting surface area; typical results are iron, folate or B12 deficiency, diarrhoea and weight loss.
- Lactase deficiency: undigested lactose is osmotically active and fermented by colonic bacteria, giving bloating, gas and watery diarrhoea.
- Pancreatic insufficiency (for example chronic pancreatitis): too little lipase causes steatorrhoea (pale, bulky, foul, floating stools) and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
- Terminal ileal disease or resection: vitamin B12 deficiency, and bile salt loss that can cause diarrhoea and fat malabsorption.
- Autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia): loss of parietal cells removes intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed even though the ileum is healthy.
- Secretory diarrhoea (for example cholera): large volumes of chloride-driven secretion; the sodium-coupled glucose transporter still works, which is why glucose-containing oral rehydration solutions are effective.

Tests follow the suspected defect.
- Blood tests: full blood count (anaemia, macrocytosis), ferritin, B12, folate, vitamin D and albumin show which nutrients are deficient.
- Coeliac disease: tissue transglutaminase antibodies are a first test and a small-bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy.
- Faecal tests: faecal elastase is low in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency; the appearance of steatorrhoea supports fat malabsorption.
- Breath tests can detect lactose malabsorption.
- Endoscopy and imaging show structural disease, such as strictures or inflammation in the terminal ileum.

Clinical application
A 28-year-old woman has had tiredness, loose pale stools and bloating for months. She is anaemic with a low ferritin and low folate. Villous atrophy on duodenal biopsy explains both the malabsorption and the pattern of deficiency: iron and folate are absorbed in the proximal small intestine, the very region that coeliac disease damages first.
Gastroenteritis in a child teaches the opposite lesson. Even when diarrhoea is severe, glucose and sodium in an oral rehydration solution are absorbed together by the same cotransporter and draw water with them, which is why this simple solution can replace losses.

Common misconceptions
- Students often think digestion happens mainly in the stomach. In fact most chemical digestion and nearly all absorption occur in the small intestine; the stomach starts protein digestion, stores and mixes.
- Students often think bile contains digestive enzymes. It does not: bile salts emulsify fat and form micelles, while the digesting enzyme, lipase, comes from the pancreas.
- Students often think all absorbed fat enters the blood capillaries. Long-chain fats leave as chylomicrons through lacteals into lymph and reach the blood via the thoracic duct.
- Students often think diarrhoea means the gut absorbs nothing. Sodium-coupled glucose uptake persists in many causes of diarrhoea, which is the basis of oral rehydration.
- Students often think vitamin B12 deficiency means a poor diet. It is usually malabsorption: lack of intrinsic factor or terminal ileal disease.

notes.overview: The liver is both a metabolic factory and the source of bile; the pancreas supplies digestive enzymes and bicarbonate. This topic links liver structure to function, follows bilirubin from red-cell breakdown to stool, separates the three types of jaundice, and shows how liver blood tests are read.
objectives: Describe the liver's dual blood supply and its main functions.
Trace bilirubin from haem to stercobilin and distinguish pre-hepatic, hepatic and post-hepatic jaundice.
Explain what bile contains and how bile salts are recycled.
Distinguish tests of liver injury from tests of liver function.
Interpret hepatitic and cholestatic patterns of liver blood tests.

The liver receives roughly three-quarters of its blood from the hepatic portal vein (nutrient-rich) and the rest from the hepatic artery (approximate). Blood flows through porous sinusoids between plates of hepatocytes (about 80% of liver volume) to the central vein of each lobule, while bile flows the opposite way in canaliculi towards the bile duct. The portal triad at the edge of each lobule contains a branch of the portal vein, the hepatic artery and a bile duct.
Hepatocytes carry out many roles:
- Carbohydrate: store glycogen, release glucose by glycogenolysis and make it by gluconeogenesis.
- Fat: make lipoproteins and cholesterol, and convert fatty acids to ketone bodies in fasting.
- Protein: make albumin and most clotting factors, and convert ammonia to urea.
- Bile: about 1 L a day of an alkaline fluid containing bile salts, phospholipids, cholesterol, bilirubin and electrolytes.
- Detoxification and drug metabolism, and storage of vitamins and iron.
The gallbladder stores bile and concentrates it up to about tenfold; CCK makes it contract. The pancreas supplies enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases) from acinar cells and bicarbonate-rich fluid from duct cells, controlled by secretin and CCK.

Bilirubin comes mainly from haem in ageing red cells.
1. Haem is converted to biliverdin and then to unconjugated bilirubin, which is lipid-soluble and travels bound to albumin.
2. Hepatocytes take it up and conjugate it with glucuronic acid, making it water-soluble.
3. Conjugated bilirubin is secreted into bile and enters the duodenum.
4. Gut bacteria convert it to urobilinogen and then mostly to stercobilin, which colours the stool brown; a little urobilinogen is reabsorbed and appears in urine.
Bile salts (made from cholesterol) emulsify fat; about 95% (approximate) are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver in portal blood, so a small pool is reused many times a day.

- Pre-hepatic: excess haemolysis overwhelms conjugation, so unconjugated bilirubin rises. The urine is not dark because albumin-bound bilirubin is not filtered.
- Hepatic: damaged hepatocytes take up, conjugate or secrete bilirubin poorly, and both forms may rise.
- Post-hepatic (obstructive): blocked bile flow raises conjugated bilirubin, which is water-soluble and appears in urine (dark urine); stools are pale because little bilirubin reaches the gut, and retained bile salts cause itch.

- Gilbert's syndrome: a common (about 5–8% of people) harmless reduction in conjugation. Mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia appears with fasting or illness, with normal liver enzymes and no haemolysis.
- Gallstones: biliary colic (pain when a stone obstructs the cystic duct), cholecystitis, or obstructive jaundice if a stone lodges in the common bile duct; infection above an obstruction (cholangitis) causes fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain.
- Acute pancreatitis: gallstones and alcohol are leading causes; enzymes activated inside the gland digest it, causing severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, with raised serum amylase or lipase.
- Chronic liver disease: loss of function gives low albumin, a prolonged prothrombin time, ascites, spider naevi, and confusion (hepatic encephalopathy) when ammonia is not cleared.

- Markers of injury: ALT and AST (hepatocytes), ALP and GGT (bile ducts).
- Markers of function: bilirubin, albumin and prothrombin time or INR.
- Patterns: hepatitic (ALT and AST raised most), cholestatic (ALP and GGT raised most) or isolated raised bilirubin.
- ALP also comes from bone and is raised in growing children and pregnancy; a raised GGT shows that ALP is probably hepatic because GGT is not found in bone.
- An AST:ALT ratio above 1 suggests advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis.
- Albumin falls in chronic liver disease but also in inflammation, nephrotic syndrome and malnutrition, so it is not specific.
Typical adult UK ranges (they vary by laboratory): ALT about 10–40 U/L, ALP about 30–130 U/L, GGT up to about 50–60 U/L (higher in men), bilirubin up to about 21 µmol/L, albumin about 35–50 g/L.

The dark urine is conjugated bilirubin filtered by the kidney, the pale stool is the lack of bilirubin reaching the gut, and the itch is retained bile salts. Ultrasound is a sensible first test to look for dilated bile ducts and stones, because finding or excluding obstruction decides the next steps.

The BSG guideline advises repeating the tests on a fasting sample with a full blood count and split bilirubin, and then reassurance once haemolysis is excluded.

- Students often think jaundice always means liver disease. Haemolysis (pre-hepatic), Gilbert's syndrome and bile duct obstruction (post-hepatic) all cause jaundice.
- Students often think all bilirubin appears in the urine. Only conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble; albumin-bound unconjugated bilirubin is not filtered.

notes.overview: Nutrition links what is eaten to health. This topic covers nutrient classes and energy balance, UK dietary targets for prevention, deficiency states, and how nutritional status is measured and screened with BMI, percentage weight loss and the MUST tool, including the physiology behind refeeding syndrome.
objectives: Distinguish macronutrients and micronutrients and state their roles.
Calculate BMI and percentage weight loss and interpret them.
State current UK dietary targets for saturated fat, free sugars, fibre and salt.
Score the MUST tool and explain its management categories.
Explain why refeeding can cause hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and thiamine depletion.

sections.body:
Macronutrients supply energy and building blocks: carbohydrate and protein give about 4 kcal per gram, fat about 9 kcal per gram and alcohol about 7 kcal per gram (standard textbook values). Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals needed in small amounts. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed with dietary fat and stored; water-soluble vitamins (B group and C) are mostly not stored in large amounts and excess is lost in urine; vitamin B12 is the main exception, with liver stores lasting years. Fibre is non-digestible plant material that adds bulk, feeds colonic bacteria and slows glucose absorption.
Body weight is stable when energy intake equals energy expenditure. Expenditure has three parts: basal metabolic rate (the largest share), the thermic effect of food and physical activity. A sustained surplus is stored mostly as triglyceride in adipose tissue; a sustained deficit uses up fat and then lean tissue.
Body mass index (BMI) = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². It is a screening measure, not a diagnosis: it does not distinguish fat from muscle, ignores where fat is distributed, and the cut-offs are not equally valid in every ethnic group.

Diet influences disease through energy balance and specific nutrients.
- Energy surplus leads to adiposity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, hypertension and fatty liver.
- High salt intake raises blood pressure by retaining sodium and water.
- Free sugars add energy with little satiety and cause dental caries.
- Saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol; fibre is associated with lower bowel and cardiovascular risk.
Refeeding syndrome. In prolonged starvation insulin is low and the body runs on fat and ketones. Intracellular phosphate, potassium and magnesium become depleted although plasma levels may look normal. When feeding restarts, carbohydrate raises insulin, which drives glucose, phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells (glycolysis and ATP synthesis need phosphate) and promotes sodium and water retention. Plasma phosphate, potassium and magnesium fall abruptly and thiamine, a cofactor for glucose metabolism, is used up. Consequences include arrhythmias, heart failure, muscle weakness, confusion, seizures and Wernicke's encephalopathy.

- Iron: microcytic anaemia. Vitamin B12 or folate: macrocytic anaemia (B12 also causes neuropathy; folate deficiency in early pregnancy raises neural tube defect risk).
- Vitamin D: rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
- Vitamin C: scurvy (bleeding gums, bruising, poor wound healing).
- Thiamine (B1): Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, abnormal eye movements) and Korsakoff syndrome, especially in alcohol dependence.
- Niacin (B3): pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia).
- Vitamin K: bleeding from low clotting factors. Vitamin A: night blindness.
- Protein–energy malnutrition: wasting (marasmus), or oedema (kwashiorkor), which is classically attributed to low albumin reducing plasma oncotic pressure, although the mechanism is debated.

sections.h: Assessing nutritional status and screening (UK guidance)
sections.body:
Assessment combines dietary history, weight, height, BMI and percentage weight loss = (usual weight − current weight) ÷ usual weight × 100. Albumin and CRP are poor markers of nutritional status because they change with inflammation.
NICE CG32 describes a person as malnourished if BMI is below 18.5 kg/m², or unintentional weight loss exceeds 10% in the last 3–6 months, or BMI is below 20 with unintentional weight loss over 5% in 3–6 months. Hospital inpatients should be screened on admission and outpatients at their first clinic appointment.
BAPEN's MUST has five steps: (1) BMI score (above 20 = 0, 18.5–20 = 1, below 18.5 = 2); (2) unplanned weight loss in 3–6 months (below 5% = 0, 5–10% = 1, above 10% = 2); (3) acute disease effect (2 if acutely ill and there has been, or is likely to be, no intake for more than 5 days); (4) add the scores: 0 low, 1 medium, 2 or more high risk; (5) manage: low risk is 'routine clinical care' with repeat screening; medium risk is 'observe', documenting dietary intake for 3 days and acting if intake is inadequate; high risk is 'treat' (refer to a dietitian or nutrition support team or follow local policy, set goals, and monitor and review the care plan); in all categories treat the underlying condition.

sections.h: Dietary targets and refeeding risk (UK guidance)
sections.body:
Public Health England's Government Dietary Recommendations (2016; check for updates) give adult targets: saturated fat no more than 11% of food energy, free sugars no more than 5% of energy, fibre 30 g a day, salt less than 6 g a day, and at least 50% of energy from carbohydrate. GOV.UK (June 2026) restates the free sugars (5%) and salt (6 g) figures. Worked example: 5% of a 2,000 kcal day is 100 kcal, which at 4 kcal per gram is 25 g of free sugars.
NICE CG32 lists high risk of refeeding problems as one or more of: BMI below 16, unintentional weight loss over 15% in 3–6 months, little or no intake for more than 10 days, or low potassium, phosphate or magnesium before feeding; or two or more of: BMI below 18.5, weight loss over 10%, little intake for more than 5 days, or a history of alcohol misuse or certain drugs (insulin, chemotherapy, antacids, diuretics). People at high risk have feeding reintroduced cautiously, with electrolyte monitoring and thiamine and vitamin supplementation (no doses given here).

A 74-year-old widow living alone has lost weight from 64 kg to 56 kg over four months and is 1.60 m tall. Her BMI is 56 ÷ 1.60² = 21.9 (score 0), but she has lost 8 ÷ 64 = 12.5% of her weight (score 2). She is not acutely ill (score 0), so the MUST total is 2: high risk. A normal BMI can therefore hide serious malnutrition, which is why weight loss is part of the tool. The plan is to find the cause of the weight loss, involve a dietitian and set goals, while recognising that if she has been eating very little for days, nutrition should be rebuilt cautiously because of refeeding risk.

- Students often think a normal BMI means good nutrition. In fact someone can have a normal BMI and still have major unintentional weight loss or micronutrient deficiency.

- Students often think 'sugar' targets mean all sugars. The 5% target is for free sugars (added sugars and those in honey, syrups and juices), not sugars inside whole fruit and milk.

notes.h: Energy metabolism: fed, fasting and starvation
notes.overview: Cells need a constant supply of ATP, and the body switches fuels with the feeding cycle. This topic covers the main pathways for carbohydrate, fat and protein, shows how the liver makes glucose and ketones, and explains how insulin and glucagon steer the fed, fasting and starvation states.
objectives: Outline glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation and where each occurs.
Explain why fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose but can form ketone bodies.
Describe the fed, post-absorptive and prolonged fasting states and the hormones that control them.
Explain how lactic acidosis and ketosis arise.

The islets of Langerhans contain beta cells (insulin), alpha cells (glucagon) and delta cells (somatostatin, which inhibits both).

Insulin is the anabolic 'fed' hormone:
- Muscle and fat: it inserts GLUT4 transporters so glucose uptake rises; muscle stores glycogen and makes protein.
- Liver: it promotes glycogen synthesis and lipogenesis and suppresses glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
- Adipose tissue: it promotes triglyceride storage and suppresses lipolysis, which restrains ketone production.
- It drives potassium into cells.
Glucagon is released as glucose falls and acts mainly on the liver to increase glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and to promote ketogenesis. Adrenaline, cortisol and growth hormone also raise glucose (counter-regulatory hormones).

Diabetes mellitus is chronic hyperglycaemia from deficient insulin action.
- Type 1: autoimmune destruction of beta cells causes absolute insulin deficiency. Onset is usually over weeks, often in younger people, with weight loss and a risk of ketoacidosis; insulin is essential for life.
- Type 2: insulin resistance (strongly linked to excess adiposity) with a beta-cell response that becomes inadequate over time. Onset is gradual and it may be found incidentally.
- Other types include gestational diabetes, monogenic diabetes, pancreatic disease and drug-induced diabetes.
Symptoms arise from osmotic effects. When plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold (roughly 10 mmol/L; approximate), glucose spills into the urine and draws water with it, causing polyuria, thirst, dehydration, weight loss, blurred vision and recurrent infections. Chronic hyperglycaemia damages small vessels (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and large vessels (coronary, cerebral and peripheral arterial disease).
SGLT2 inhibitors block glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule, lowering blood glucose through glycosuria.

notes.h: Body fluid compartments, osmolality and water balance
notes.overview: Water crosses most membranes freely, so the number of dissolved particles in each compartment decides where it goes. This topic covers compartment sizes, osmolality and effective osmoles, capillary forces and oedema, how ADH and thirst control water balance, and how to read sodium disorders and U&E results.
objectives: Describe the fluid compartments and the distribution of sodium and potassium between them.
Calculate plasma osmolality and distinguish effective from ineffective osmoles.
Explain how osmoreceptors, ADH and thirst control water balance.
Explain the Starling forces behind oedema.
Interpret sodium disorders and a urea and electrolytes (U&E) result.

sections.body:
Total body water is about 60% of body mass in an adult man (lower in women and older people, who have relatively more fat and less muscle; approximate). In a 70 kg man that is about 42 L. Roughly two-thirds is intracellular (ICF, about 28 L) and one-third extracellular (ECF, about 14 L); plasma is about a fifth to a quarter of the ECF (roughly 3–3.5 L) and the remainder is interstitial fluid.
Membranes and the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase give the compartments different ions: the ECF is rich in sodium and chloride, the ICF in potassium, phosphate and protein, and plasma contains more protein than interstitial fluid.
Water crosses membranes freely, so it moves to equalise osmolality (solute particles per kilogram of water), typically about 285–295 mOsm/kg (varies by laboratory). Sodium and its anions are the main effective osmoles of the ECF: they cannot cross cell membranes, so they hold water in the ECF. Urea crosses membranes freely and is an ineffective osmole; glucose becomes effective when insulin is lacking. Plasma osmolality can be estimated as 2 × [Na⁺] + [glucose] + [urea] (mmol/L): for sodium 140, glucose 5 and urea 5 mmol/L this is 290 mOsm/kg.
Across capillaries, fluid leaves at the arteriolar end because hydrostatic pressure exceeds plasma oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure, mostly due to albumin, and, in the classical description, returns at the venular end, with lymphatics draining the excess. The revised Starling principle holds that in most tissues little fluid is reabsorbed at the venular end and lymph returns most of it; either way, the balance of hydrostatic and oncotic pressure sets net filtration.

Daily water intake and output are each roughly 2.5 L in a typical adult (approximate): intake from drinks, food and metabolic water; output mostly as urine, plus sweat, faeces and insensible losses from skin and breath.
Water balance sets plasma osmolality, and so plasma sodium concentration. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a small rise in osmolality and trigger two responses: thirst, and release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary. ADH acts on the collecting duct, inserting aquaporin-2 water channels so that water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced. When osmolality falls, ADH release stops, the collecting duct becomes impermeable to water and dilute urine is produced. A large fall in blood volume or pressure can also stimulate ADH, even when osmolality is low.
Two classic disorders: in SIADH, ADH is released inappropriately, water is retained and plasma sodium falls; in diabetes insipidus, ADH is lacking or ineffective, so large volumes of dilute urine are lost and plasma sodium rises if water intake cannot keep up.

- Dehydration: thirst, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, postural hypotension, low urine output and concentrated urine. Severe volume loss reduces kidney perfusion and can cause pre-renal acute kidney injury.
- Hyponatraemia (low plasma sodium) reflects too much water relative to sodium. It is classified by volume status: hypovolaemic (diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea), euvolaemic (SIADH, excess water intake) or hypervolaemic (heart failure, cirrhosis). Symptoms include headache, nausea, confusion and seizures; correcting too quickly risks osmotic demyelination.
- Hypernatraemia (high plasma sodium) reflects a water deficit relative to sodium: older or confused people who cannot drink, fever, or diabetes insipidus. Brain cells shrink as water leaves them.
- Oedema forms when capillary hydrostatic pressure rises (heart failure), plasma albumin falls (nephrotic syndrome, liver disease), capillaries become leaky (inflammation) or lymph drainage fails.

Typical adult UK ranges (they vary by laboratory): sodium about 133–146 mmol/L, potassium about 3.5–5.3 mmol/L, urea about 2.5–7.8 mmol/L, creatinine about 60–110 µmol/L (higher in men, lower in women).
- Calculated osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose + urea. A measured osmolality well above the calculated value suggests an unmeasured osmole such as alcohol.
- Urea:creatinine ratio (urea in mmol/L × 1000 ÷ creatinine in µmol/L) above about 100 suggests a pre-renal state, because urea is reabsorbed along with water when ADH is high; urea also rises with an upper gastrointestinal bleed or tissue catabolism.
- Hyponatraemia work-up: a low measured serum osmolality confirms true hypotonic hyponatraemia (a low calculated value alone cannot exclude pseudohyponatraemia); a urine osmolality that is not maximally dilute despite low plasma osmolality shows ADH is acting; assess volume status.
- Hyperglycaemia can lower measured sodium by drawing water out of cells, so interpret sodium with the glucose.

A 79-year-old woman with pneumonia has eaten and drunk almost nothing for three days. She is thirsty and confused, her mucous membranes are dry and her sodium is 148 mmol/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, urea 14.8 mmol/L and creatinine 128 µmol/L (baseline 80). Calculated osmolality is 2 × 148 + 5.2 + 14.8 = 316 mOsm/kg: a water deficit has concentrated the ECF and pulled water out of cells. Urea:creatinine is about 116, a pre-renal pattern.
Contrast an endurance runner who drinks large volumes of plain water and finishes with a sodium of 126 mmol/L: the water excess has diluted sodium, and ADH release (nausea, stress) limits the ability to excrete it.

- Students often think plasma sodium concentration tells you the body's total sodium or volume. It reflects water balance relative to sodium; a person can be hyponatraemic while hypovolaemic, euvolaemic or oedematous.
- Students often think urea is an important effective osmole. Because it crosses cell membranes freely, it does not hold water in the ECF.
- Students often think thirst is triggered by blood volume alone. A small rise in osmolality is the main trigger; large volume loss is a secondary one.
- Students often think oedema means too much plasma volume. Plasma volume may be low (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis) while fluid leaks into tissues.

notes.h: Sodium, potassium, volume control and IV fluid principles
notes.overview: Sodium content sets ECF volume, and potassium sets excitability. This topic covers the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and natriuretic peptide, how potassium is distributed and regulated, the clinical picture of hypovolaemia and potassium disorders, and the NICE principles for prescribing IV fluids safely.
objectives: Explain how renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone and ANP control sodium and ECF volume.

sections.h: Sodium, volume and the hormones that control them
sections.body:
Because water follows sodium, the amount of sodium in the body determines ECF volume. When blood pressure or renal perfusion falls, or sympathetic activity rises, juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Renin leads to angiotensin II, which causes vasoconstriction, stimulates thirst and drives aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex. Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct to increase sodium reabsorption (and water with it) and potassium secretion.
Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), released when the atria are stretched by a high volume, opposes this: it promotes sodium excretion and so lowers volume and pressure.
Keep two systems distinct. Osmolality (water balance) is controlled by ADH and thirst; ECF volume (sodium balance) by the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, ANP, sympathetic activity and renal haemodynamics. Loop and thiazide diuretics act by blocking tubular sodium transport, so sodium and water are lost together.

About 98% of body potassium is intracellular (approximate), so plasma potassium is only a small, tightly regulated fraction of the total. The ratio of intracellular to extracellular potassium sets the resting membrane potential of nerve, muscle and heart cells.
- Shifts into cells: insulin, β-adrenergic stimulation and alkalosis.
- Shifts out of cells: lack of insulin, acidosis, cell breakdown and hyperosmolality.
- Excretion: filtered potassium is mostly reabsorbed early in the nephron, and the amount excreted is set in the distal tubule and collecting duct, where aldosterone increases potassium secretion. Anything that reduces distal sodium delivery or aldosterone effect (acute kidney injury, ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics) predisposes to hyperkalaemia.
Hyperkalaemia partially depolarises excitable cells; they cannot repolarise properly, so cardiac conduction slows and fatal arrhythmias can occur. Hypokalaemia hyperpolarises cells, causing weakness and arrhythmias.

- Hypovolaemia (low ECF volume): thirst, tachycardia, postural hypotension, low JVP, reduced skin turgor, cool peripheries, prolonged capillary refill and low urine output; causes include bleeding, vomiting, diarrhoea, burns and diuretics.
- Hypervolaemia (high ECF volume): raised JVP, oedema, crackles from pulmonary oedema and weight gain, as in heart failure, cirrhosis and kidney disease.
- Hyperkalaemia: often silent until the ECG changes (tall peaked T waves, flattened P waves, widened QRS); common causes are acute kidney injury, potassium-sparing drugs, ACE inhibitors and acidosis.
- Hypokalaemia: weakness, cramps, ectopic beats; common causes are loop and thiazide diuretics, vomiting and diarrhoea.

NICE guideline CG174, now titled for over-16s in hospital, was published in 2013 and its text last updated in 2017; a 2020 surveillance review found no new evidence affecting its recommendations. Its main principles are:
- Assess fluid and electrolyte needs at every ward review and use IV fluids only when oral or enteral routes cannot meet them; stop them as soon as possible.
- Think in five categories: resuscitation, routine maintenance, replacement of existing deficits or ongoing losses, redistribution, and reassessment.
- For resuscitation use crystalloids that contain sodium 130–154 mmol/L; tetrastarch is not used.
- Routine maintenance starts as a restricted prescription of water, electrolytes (including potassium) and glucose, adjusted for age, frailty, renal or cardiac impairment and nutritional risk, including risk of refeeding syndrome.
- Potassium is not added directly to fluid bags; after fluids containing chloride above 120 mmol/L (such as 0.9% sodium chloride), monitor serum chloride daily.
- Reassess clinical fluid status, urea, creatinine and electrolytes, and fluid balance charts at least daily, weigh the patient twice weekly, and seek expert help for complex cases.
No volumes or rates are given here, because they depend on the individual patient and local protocol.

A man with a haemorrhage loses about a litre of blood. Baroreceptors detect the fall in pressure, sympathetic activity rises (tachycardia, vasoconstriction) and renal hypoperfusion releases renin, so angiotensin II and aldosterone retain sodium and water; ADH is released because the volume fall is large. Together these defend perfusion; a rising heart rate and a narrowing pulse pressure are signs of this compensation, and a falling systolic pressure shows it is failing.
A patient with chronic kidney disease taking an ACE inhibitor and a potassium supplement, with a plasma potassium of 6.8 mmol/L and peaked T waves on the ECG, shows how reduced renal potassium excretion plus reduced aldosterone effect leads to dangerous hyperkalaemia.

- Students often think ADH controls blood volume directly. It mainly sets water balance and osmolality; sodium, through the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and ANP, determines ECF volume.
- Students often think plasma potassium reflects body stores. It does not: shifts between cells and plasma can change the plasma level without changing total potassium.
- Students often think giving more IV fluid is always safer. Excess fluid causes oedema and harm, which is why CG174 emphasises assessment, restricted maintenance and daily review.
- Students often think all fluids containing sodium are equivalent. Composition (for example chloride content) matters for acid–base balance and monitoring.

notes.h: The kidney: filtration, tubular function and kidney injury
notes.overview: The kidney filters about 180 litres of plasma a day and then reclaims almost all of it. This topic covers the nephron, the forces behind filtration and how the kidney protects GFR, tubular handling, clearance calculations, and how acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease are detected and staged.
objectives: Describe the nephron and the forces that produce glomerular filtration.
Explain how autoregulation and the tubuloglomerular feedback system keep GFR stable, and how drugs can disturb it.
Summarise what each part of the tubule does.
Calculate clearance and explain the strengths and limits of creatinine as a marker of GFR.
Apply the NICE NG148 criteria and the UK Kidney Association stages for acute kidney injury, and the NG203 categories for chronic kidney disease.

sections.body:
Each kidney contains about a million nephrons. Blood enters the glomerulus through the afferent arteriole and leaves through the efferent arteriole. The filtration barrier has three layers: fenestrated endothelium, a basement membrane and the slit diaphragms between podocyte foot processes. It lets water and small solutes through but holds back most albumin and all cells, so heavy proteinuria, or blood together with protein in the urine, points to glomerular damage (blood alone can come from anywhere in the urinary tract).
Filtration is driven by Starling forces. Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (about 55 mmHg) pushes fluid out; capsular hydrostatic pressure (about 15 mmHg) and capillary oncotic pressure (about 30 mmHg) oppose it, so the net filtration pressure is 55 − (15 + 30) = 10 mmHg (approximate values). The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is about 125 mL/min, roughly 180 L/day, in a healthy young adult.
GFR is kept steady across a wide range of arterial pressure (roughly 80–180 mmHg, approximate) by autoregulation: the myogenic response of the afferent arteriole, and tubuloglomerular feedback, in which the macula densa senses the delivery of sodium chloride to the distal tubule and adjusts afferent tone and renin release by the juxtaglomerular cells.

- Proximal tubule: reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered sodium and water, and essentially all glucose and amino acids (glucose transport saturates at a plasma concentration of roughly 10 mmol/L, approximate, after which glucose appears in the urine). Most filtered bicarbonate is reclaimed here.
- Loop of Henle: the descending limb is permeable to water and the thick ascending limb reabsorbs sodium, potassium and chloride through the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter without water, building the medullary gradient (target of loop diuretics).
- Distal tubule: further sodium reabsorption through the sodium–chloride cotransporter (target of thiazide diuretics) and calcium handling.
- Collecting duct: aldosterone controls sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion; ADH controls water permeability; intercalated cells secrete acid.
Clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute: C = U × V ÷ P, where U is the urine concentration, V the urine flow rate and P the plasma concentration. Example: U = 6 mmol/L, V = 2 mL/min and P = 0.1 mmol/L give C = 6 × 2 ÷ 0.1 = 120 mL/min. For a substance that is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, clearance equals GFR. - Pre-renal: reduced perfusion (hypovolaemia, sepsis, heart failure, and drugs that interfere with autoregulation). The tubules are intact, so urine is concentrated and sodium is conserved.
- Intrinsic: damage to the glomerulus (nephritis), tubule (acute tubular necrosis, often after prolonged hypoperfusion or toxins) or interstitium.
- Post-renal: obstruction of the urinary tract, for example from prostate enlargement or stones; the pressure in the capsule rises and opposes filtration.
Two drug groups matter for autoregulation. When perfusion is low, prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, which maintains glomerular pressure. NSAIDs remove the first and ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers the second, so GFR can fall sharply, especially with diuretics and volume depletion (the so-called "triple whammy").
Late features of kidney failure include oedema, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, uraemic symptoms and anaemia (mainly from reduced erythropoietin production).

sections.body:
NICE NG148 recommends identifying acute kidney injury (AKI) when any one of these is present: a rise in serum creatinine of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours; a rise of 50% or more known or presumed to have occurred within the past 7 days; or a fall in urine output to below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours. The UK Kidney Association algorithm stages AKI by the ratio of current to baseline creatinine: stage 1 is 1.5–1.9 times baseline (or a rise of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours), stage 2 is 2.0–2.9 times, and stage 3 is 3.0 times or more (stage 3 also includes a rise above 1.5 times baseline to more than 354 µmol/L, and the guidance gives urine output bands as well).

The first steps are to assess volume status, review the nephrotoxic drugs and seek and treat the cause, then monitor urine output and potassium.

notes.overview: Normal cell function depends on a tightly held blood pH. This topic covers buffers and the Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship, how the lungs and kidneys respond, the four primary disorders with their compensation, and a stepwise way to read an arterial blood gas including the anion gap.
objectives: Explain the buffer systems and the time scales over which buffers, lungs and kidneys respond.
Use the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation to calculate pH from bicarbonate and carbon dioxide.
Classify the four primary acid–base disorders and their compensation.
Calculate and interpret the anion gap and the expected respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis.
Interpret an arterial blood gas step by step.

sections.h: pH, buffers and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
sections.body:
Arterial pH is held at about 7.35–7.45 (hydrogen ion concentration about 35–45 nmol/L); typical adult UK arterial ranges, which vary by laboratory, are PaCO₂ about 4.7–6.0 kPa and bicarbonate about 22–29 mmol/L.
Buffers resist pH change. The bicarbonate system (CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻) is the main buffer of extracellular fluid and is powerful because the lungs control CO₂ and the kidneys control bicarbonate. Proteins (including haemoglobin) and phosphate buffer mainly inside cells and in urine.
The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻] ÷ (0.225 × PaCO₂)), with bicarbonate in mmol/L and PaCO₂ in kPa. Example: bicarbonate 24 mmol/L and PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa give 0.225 × 5.3 = 1.19, a ratio of 20.1 to 1, log₁₀ 1.30, so pH 7.40. A ratio of about 20:1 is normal; pH falls if the ratio falls (metabolic acidosis or CO₂ retention) and rises if it increases.
Responses act on different time scales: buffers within seconds, the lungs within minutes (changing PaCO₂) and the kidneys over hours to days (changing acid excretion and bicarbonate reabsorption).

sections.h: How the lungs and kidneys correct pH
sections.body:
Central chemoreceptors respond to a rise in CO₂ (through brain extracellular pH) and peripheral chemoreceptors respond to low pH, driving a higher ventilation rate; a rising pH slows breathing.
In the kidney, the proximal tubule reclaims most filtered bicarbonate through carbonic anhydrase-dependent secretion of H⁺. Intercalated cells of the collecting duct secrete additional H⁺, which is buffered in the urine by phosphate and ammonia, generating new bicarbonate for the blood. In acidosis the kidney excretes more acid and makes more ammonia; in alkalosis it excretes bicarbonate.
Compensation reduces but does not normally completely correct the change in pH.

- Metabolic acidosis: low bicarbonate. Compensation is hyperventilation, lowering PaCO₂ (Kussmaul breathing). Winter's formula estimates the expected PaCO₂ in mmHg as 1.5 × bicarbonate + 8, ± 2 (divide by 7.5 for kPa). A PaCO₂ above the range suggests an additional respiratory problem, and one below it a coexisting respiratory alkalosis.
- Metabolic alkalosis: high bicarbonate, for example after vomiting (loss of gastric acid, volume contraction, potassium loss). Compensation is hypoventilation, which is limited by the need to oxygenate.
- Respiratory acidosis: high PaCO₂ from hypoventilation (COPD, sedation, neuromuscular weakness). Over days the kidney retains bicarbonate, so a raised bicarbonate suggests chronicity.
- Respiratory alkalosis: low PaCO₂ from hyperventilation (anxiety, pain, pulmonary embolism, early salicylate toxicity).
Anion gap = sodium − (chloride + bicarbonate), with a typical range of roughly 8–16 mmol/L that varies by laboratory and by whether potassium is included. A raised gap indicates unmeasured anions: lactate, ketones, uraemia or toxins. A normal gap acidosis with high chloride (hyperchloraemic) occurs with diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis and large volumes of 0.9% sodium chloride.

sections.h: A stepwise approach to a blood gas
sections.body:
1. Is the patient acidaemic (pH below 7.35) or alkalaemic (above 7.45)?
2. What is the primary process: if acidaemic, a low bicarbonate means metabolic and a high PaCO₂ means respiratory; if alkalaemic, a high bicarbonate means metabolic and a low PaCO₂ means respiratory.
3. Is compensation present and appropriate? In metabolic acidosis apply Winter's formula; in chronic respiratory acidosis expect a raised bicarbonate.
4. In a metabolic acidosis calculate the anion gap.
5. Check oxygenation (PaO₂ typically above about 10.5 kPa on air, varying by laboratory) and relate everything to the clinical picture.
pH is rarely fully normal in a single compensated disorder; a normal pH with grossly abnormal PaCO₂ and bicarbonate suggests a mixed disorder.

A 19-year-old with diabetic ketoacidosis has pH 7.12, PaCO₂ 2.4 kPa and bicarbonate 5.6 mmol/L; sodium is 134 and chloride 98 mmol/L. Check: 0.225 × 2.4 = 0.54; 5.6 ÷ 0.54 = 10.4; log₁₀ 1.02, so pH 7.12. The gap is 134 − 98 − 5.6 = 30.4 mmol/L, raised. Winter's formula gives 1.5 × 5.6 + 8 = 16.4 mmHg ± 2, or 1.9–2.5 kPa; the measured 2.4 kPa lies within it, so respiratory compensation is appropriate.
By contrast, a patient with COPD, pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 8.6 kPa, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L and PaO₂ 7.9 kPa has a respiratory acidosis with renal compensation.

- Students often think a normal pH excludes an acid–base disorder. Compensation, or opposing disorders, can bring pH close to normal.
- Students often think compensation fully corrects pH. It limits the change but rarely normalises it.
- Students often think vomiting causes alkalosis by losing bicarbonate. It loses gastric hydrochloric acid, leaving excess bicarbonate.
- Students often think the rapid deep breathing in diabetic ketoacidosis is a respiratory problem. It is appropriate compensation for a metabolic acidosis.

pH, buffers and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
Arterial pH is held at about 7.35–7.45 (hydrogen ion concentration about 35–45 nmol/L); typical adult UK arterial ranges, which vary by laboratory, are PaCO₂ about 4.7–6.0 kPa and bicarbonate about 22–29 mmol/L.
Buffers resist pH change. The bicarbonate system (CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻) is the main buffer of extracellular fluid and is powerful because the lungs control CO₂ and the kidneys control bicarbonate. Proteins (including haemoglobin) and phosphate buffer mainly inside cells and in urine.
The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻] ÷ (0.225 × PaCO₂)), with bicarbonate in mmol/L and PaCO₂ in kPa. Example: bicarbonate 24 mmol/L and PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa give 0.225 × 5.3 = 1.19, a ratio of 20.1 to 1, log₁₀ 1.30, so pH 7.40. A ratio of about 20:1 is normal; pH falls if the ratio falls (metabolic acidosis or CO₂ retention) and rises if it increases.
Responses act on different time scales: buffers within seconds, the lungs within minutes (changing PaCO₂) and the kidneys over hours to days (changing acid excretion and bicarbonate reabsorption).

How the lungs and kidneys correct pH
Central chemoreceptors respond to a rise in CO₂ (through brain extracellular pH) and peripheral chemoreceptors respond to low pH, driving a higher ventilation rate; a rising pH slows breathing.
In the kidney, the proximal tubule reclaims most filtered bicarbonate through carbonic anhydrase-dependent secretion of H⁺. Intercalated cells of the collecting duct secrete additional H⁺, which is buffered in the urine by phosphate and ammonia, generating new bicarbonate for the blood. In acidosis the kidney excretes more acid and makes more ammonia; in alkalosis it excretes bicarbonate.
Compensation reduces but does not normally completely correct the change in pH.

The four primary disorders
- Metabolic acidosis: low bicarbonate. Compensation is hyperventilation, lowering PaCO₂ (Kussmaul breathing). Winter's formula estimates the expected PaCO₂ in mmHg as 1.5 × bicarbonate + 8, ± 2 (divide by 7.5 for kPa). A PaCO₂ above the range suggests an additional respiratory problem, and one below it a coexisting respiratory alkalosis.
- Metabolic alkalosis: high bicarbonate, for example after vomiting (loss of gastric acid, volume contraction, potassium loss). Compensation is hypoventilation, which is limited by the need to oxygenate.
- Respiratory acidosis: high PaCO₂ from hypoventilation (COPD, sedation, neuromuscular weakness). Over days the kidney retains bicarbonate, so a raised bicarbonate suggests chronicity.
- Respiratory alkalosis: low PaCO₂ from hyperventilation (anxiety, pain, pulmonary embolism, early salicylate toxicity).
Anion gap = sodium − (chloride + bicarbonate), with a typical range of roughly 8–16 mmol/L that varies by laboratory and by whether potassium is included. A raised gap indicates unmeasured anions: lactate, ketones, uraemia or toxins. A normal gap acidosis with high chloride (hyperchloraemic) occurs with diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis and large volumes of 0.9% sodium chloride.

A stepwise approach to a blood gas
1. Is the patient acidaemic (pH below 7.35) or alkalaemic (above 7.45)?
2. What is the primary process: if acidaemic, a low bicarbonate means metabolic and a high PaCO₂ means respiratory; if alkalaemic, a high bicarbonate means metabolic and a low PaCO₂ means respiratory.
3. Is compensation present and appropriate? In metabolic acidosis apply Winter's formula; in chronic respiratory acidosis expect a raised bicarbonate.
4. In a metabolic acidosis calculate the anion gap.
5. Check oxygenation (PaO₂ typically above about 10.5 kPa on air, varying by laboratory) and relate everything to the clinical picture.
pH is rarely fully normal in a single compensated disorder; a normal pH with grossly abnormal PaCO₂ and bicarbonate suggests a mixed disorder.

Clinical application
A 19-year-old with diabetic ketoacidosis has pH 7.12, PaCO₂ 2.4 kPa and bicarbonate 5.6 mmol/L; sodium is 134 and chloride 98 mmol/L. Check: 0.225 × 2.4 = 0.54; 5.6 ÷ 0.54 = 10.4; log₁₀ 1.02, so pH 7.12. The gap is 134 − 98 − 5.6 = 30.4 mmol/L, raised. Winter's formula gives 1.5 × 5.6 + 8 = 16.4 mmHg ± 2, or 1.9–2.5 kPa; the measured 2.4 kPa lies within it, so respiratory compensation is appropriate.
By contrast, a patient with COPD, pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 8.6 kPa, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L and PaO₂ 7.9 kPa has a respiratory acidosis with renal compensation.

Common misconceptions
- Students often think a normal pH excludes an acid–base disorder. Compensation, or opposing disorders, can bring pH close to normal.
- Students often think compensation fully corrects pH. It limits the change but rarely normalises it.
- Students often think vomiting causes alkalosis by losing bicarbonate. It loses gastric hydrochloric acid, leaving excess bicarbonate.
- Students often think the rapid deep breathing in diabetic ketoacidosis is a respiratory problem. It is appropriate compensation for a metabolic acidosis.

cards.f: Four layers of the gut wall (lumen outwards)
cards.b: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa (adventitia in the oesophagus).
cards.ex: The Meissner plexus lies in the submucosa and the Auerbach plexus lies between the two muscle layers.

cards.f: Arterial supply of foregut, midgut and hindgut
cards.b: Foregut: coeliac trunk. Midgut: superior mesenteric artery. Hindgut: inferior mesenteric artery.
cards.ex: Each embryological part keeps its own artery into adult life, which also predicts where ischaemia and referred pain appear.

cards.f: How does the structure of the small intestine increase absorptive area?
cards.b: Circular folds, villi and microvilli (brush border) multiply the surface to roughly 200 m² (approximate); lacteals in the villi take up fat.
cards.ex: Each fold of the surface multiplies the area available for contact with chyme.

cards.f: Intraperitoneal versus retroperitoneal organs
cards.b: Intraperitoneal (on a mesentery, mobile): jejunum, ileum, transverse and sigmoid colon. Retroperitoneal: duodenum (mostly), pancreas, ascending and descending colon, rectum.
cards.ex: Retroperitoneal organs lie behind the peritoneum and are fixed to the posterior abdominal wall.

cards.f: Why is midgut pain felt around the umbilicus?
cards.b: Visceral afferents from midgut structures enter the cord at about T9–T11, so pain is referred to the dermatomes around the umbilicus (T10).
cards.ex: The brain localises visceral pain to the dermatome that shares the spinal segment.

cards.f: Why do absorbed nutrients and drugs meet the liver before the rest of the body?
cards.b: Gut venous blood drains through the hepatic portal vein to the liver sinusoids before reaching the systemic circulation (first-pass effect).
cards.ex: The portal system is a venous route between two capillary beds: gut then liver.

cards.f: A sudden blockage of the superior mesenteric artery threatens which parts of the gut?
cards.b: The midgut: small bowel from the distal duodenum onwards, the caecum and ascending colon, and the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.
cards.ex: Match the artery to its embryological territory.

cards.f: A plain film shows the caecum 11 cm wide. How do you read this?
cards.b: It exceeds the 9 cm guide, so the caecum is dilated (large-bowel obstruction or pseudo-obstruction); the risk of perforation rises as it distends.
cards.ex: Caecal diameter is part of the 3/6/9 rule.

cards.f: Gastrin, secretin and CCK: trigger and effect
cards.b: Gastrin: food and stretch, stimulates acid. Secretin: acid in the duodenum, stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate. CCK: fat and protein in the duodenum, stimulates pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder contraction.
cards.ex: Each hormone is released by what arrives in its part of the gut (the stomach for gastrin, the duodenum for secretin and CCK) and triggers the secretion needed to deal with it.

cards.f: Where are vitamin B12 and bile salts absorbed?
cards.b: In the terminal ileum (B12 bound to intrinsic factor; bile salts recycled in the enterohepatic circulation).
cards.ex: Specific receptors for the B12–intrinsic factor complex and bile salt transporters are concentrated in the terminal ileum.

cards.f: Why do glucose and sodium absorption go together?
cards.b: Glucose and galactose enter enterocytes on a sodium-coupled cotransporter (SGLT1) driven by the sodium gradient made by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; water follows the absorbed solute.
cards.ex: The cotransporter only works when sodium is available to move with glucose.

cards.f: How is dietary fat absorbed?
cards.b: Bile salts emulsify, lipase splits triglycerides, micelles carry fatty acids and monoglycerides to the brush border, enterocytes rebuild triglycerides into chylomicrons, which enter the lacteals and lymph.
cards.ex: Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries, so they take the lymphatic route.

cards.f: Peristalsis versus segmentation
cards.b: Peristalsis: propulsive waves moving contents along the gut. Segmentation: local circular-muscle contractions that mix contents and expose them to the epithelium, mainly in the small intestine.
cards.ex: One moves contents on; the other churns them in place.

cards.f: Why does chronic pancreatitis cause steatorrhoea more than carbohydrate malabsorption?
cards.b: Pancreatic lipase does most fat digestion with little back-up, whereas salivary amylase and brush-border carbohydrases partly compensate for lost pancreatic amylase.
cards.ex: Fat has no equally effective alternative enzyme.

cards.f: A patient develops macrocytic anaemia after terminal ileal resection. Which vitamin is deficient?
cards.b: Vitamin B12, because the B12–intrinsic factor complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
cards.ex: The stomach still makes intrinsic factor; the missing piece is the absorptive site.

cards.f: Stools are pale, bulky and float. What does this suggest?
cards.b: Steatorrhoea: fat malabsorption from a lack of lipase or bile salts, or from damaged absorptive mucosa.
cards.ex: Unabsorbed fat makes stool bulky, pale and buoyant.

cards.f: What does the portal triad contain?
cards.b: A branch of the hepatic portal vein, a branch of the hepatic artery and a bile duct.
cards.ex: The triad sits at the edge of each lobule; blood flows towards the central vein and bile flows the other way.

cards.f: Which liver blood tests reflect function rather than injury?
cards.b: Bilirubin, albumin and prothrombin time (INR). ALT, AST, ALP and GGT mainly show injury.
cards.ex: Albumin and clotting factors are made by hepatocytes, so a failing liver makes less of them.

cards.f: Trace bilirubin from haem to stool.
cards.b: Haem → biliverdin → unconjugated bilirubin (albumin-bound) → conjugated with glucuronic acid in hepatocytes → bile → gut bacteria → urobilinogen and stercobilin (brown stool).
cards.ex: Conjugation is what makes bilirubin water-soluble enough to excrete in bile.

cards.f: Pre-hepatic versus obstructive jaundice: urine and stool
cards.b: Pre-hepatic: unconjugated bilirubin, normal-coloured urine and stool. Obstructive: conjugated bilirubin, dark urine and pale stool.
cards.ex: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and is filtered; unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound.

cards.f: Why is urine dark in obstructive jaundice?
cards.b: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble, so when bile cannot leave the liver it backs up into the blood and is filtered into the urine.
cards.ex: Only the conjugated form can cross the glomerular filter.

cards.f: Why does a raised GGT help interpret a raised ALP?
cards.b: GGT is not present in bone, so a raised GGT alongside a raised ALP suggests the ALP comes from the liver or bile ducts rather than bone.
cards.ex: Both enzymes rise in bile duct disease, but only ALP rises in bone disease.

cards.f: ALT 1,200, AST 980, ALP 140, bilirubin 60. What is the pattern?
cards.b: Hepatitic: aminotransferases are raised far more than ALP, indicating acute hepatocellular injury.
cards.ex: Compare which enzyme group is raised proportionally more.

cards.f: Why can a haemolytic anaemia cause jaundice with a healthy liver?
cards.b: Red cells are broken down faster than the liver can conjugate the extra bilirubin, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates.
cards.ex: The liver's conjugation capacity is finite.

cards.f: Energy content of macronutrients
cards.b: Carbohydrate and protein about 4 kcal/g, fat about 9 kcal/g, alcohol about 7 kcal/g (standard values).
cards.ex: Fat is the most energy-dense fuel because it is the most reduced.

cards.f: UK adult dietary targets (PHE 2016)
cards.b: Saturated fat 11% of food energy or less; free sugars 5% of energy or less; fibre 30 g/day; salt under 6 g/day; at least 50% of energy from carbohydrate.
cards.ex: These are population targets set as guidance; check for updated versions.

cards.f: How does refeeding syndrome develop?
cards.b: Feeding raises insulin, driving glucose, phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and using up thiamine, so plasma phosphate, potassium and magnesium fall sharply after a period of starvation.
cards.ex: Intracellular stores were already depleted; insulin moves what remains in plasma into cells.

cards.f: Why is thiamine given when feeding restarts in someone at refeeding risk?
cards.b: Glucose metabolism needs thiamine as a cofactor and stores are often low, so a glucose load can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.
cards.ex: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and other enzymes of carbohydrate metabolism depend on thiamine.

cards.f: Fat-soluble versus water-soluble vitamins
cards.b: Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K): absorbed with fat, stored, can accumulate. Water-soluble (B group, C): mostly little stored (B12 is an exception), excess lost in urine, so regular intake is needed.
cards.ex: Solubility decides how they are absorbed, stored and lost.

cards.f: BMI 18.0, weight loss 7.7% over 3–6 months, no acute illness: MUST score?
cards.b: BMI below 18.5 scores 2, weight loss of 5–10% scores 1, no acute effect scores 0: total 3, high risk.
cards.ex: Add the three step scores; 2 or more is high risk.

cards.f: Why is serum albumin a poor test of nutritional status?
cards.b: Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant and falls in inflammation, liver disease and nephrotic syndrome, so it does not reflect recent intake reliably.
cards.ex: Its level reflects illness more than diet.

cards.f: Why does a high-salt diet raise blood pressure?
cards.b: Extra sodium retains water, expanding extracellular and blood volume and raising cardiac output and vascular resistance over time.
cards.ex: Water follows sodium.

cards.f: Net ATP and location of glycolysis
cards.b: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and gives a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose, producing pyruvate.
cards.ex: It uses 2 ATP and makes 4, so the net is 2.

cards.f: Substrates for gluconeogenesis
cards.b: Lactate, glycerol and amino acids (for example alanine, glutamine); mainly in the liver. Even-chain fatty acids are not substrates.
cards.ex: Acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation cannot be converted to pyruvate.

cards.f: Why does the liver make ketone bodies in fasting?
cards.b: Low insulin releases fatty acids from fat; β-oxidation makes more acetyl-CoA than the citric acid cycle can use, so the liver converts the excess to ketone bodies that brain and heart can use.
cards.ex: Ketones are a water-soluble fuel from fat that the brain can use.

cards.f: Why does muscle glycogen not raise blood glucose?
cards.b: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so glucose-6-phosphate cannot be released as free glucose; it is used within the muscle.
cards.ex: Mainly the liver and kidney can dephosphorylate glucose-6-phosphate.

cards.f: How does a lack of oxygen cause lactate to accumulate?
cards.b: Without oxidative phosphorylation, NADH cannot be reoxidised in mitochondria, so pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺ for glycolysis; lactate then builds up.
cards.ex: Glycolysis needs a supply of NAD⁺.

cards.f: Starvation ketosis versus DKA
cards.b: Starvation: ketones rise but insulin restrains them; glucose low or normal; pH preserved. DKA: insulin absent; high glucose; ketones very high; severe acidosis.
cards.ex: The presence or absence of insulin decides how far ketogenesis runs.

cards.f: Why can heavy alcohol intake with poor eating cause hypoglycaemia?
cards.b: Alcohol metabolism consumes NAD⁺ and inhibits gluconeogenesis, and glycogen stores are low, so the fasting liver cannot make enough glucose.
cards.ex: Gluconeogenesis is the liver's main source of glucose once glycogen is used.

cards.f: Lactate 6.5 mmol/L, bicarbonate 14, anion gap raised in septic shock: what does it show?
cards.b: A high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis due to lactate from anaerobic glycolysis in poorly perfused tissue.
cards.ex: Lactate is an unmeasured anion that replaces bicarbonate.

cards.f: Diagnostic thresholds for diabetes (UK)
cards.b: HbA1c 48 mmol/mol or more; fasting glucose 7.0 or more; 2-hour OGTT glucose 11.1 or more; random glucose 11.1 or more with symptoms. Without symptoms, repeat to confirm.
cards.ex: These are WHO-based thresholds restated by Diabetes UK; they are guidance and may be revised.

cards.f: How does a rise in glucose trigger insulin release?
cards.b: Glucose uptake and metabolism raise ATP in beta cells, closing K⁺ channels, depolarising the cell, opening Ca²⁺ channels, and calcium triggers insulin exocytosis.
cards.ex: Metabolism of glucose is coupled to the membrane potential.

cards.f: Why does insulin restrain ketone production?
cards.b: Insulin suppresses lipolysis in adipose tissue, so fewer fatty acids reach the liver for conversion to ketone bodies.
cards.ex: Ketones are made from fatty acids released by lipolysis.

cards.f: Type 1 versus type 2 diabetes mechanism
cards.b: Type 1: autoimmune beta-cell destruction, absolute insulin deficiency. Type 2: insulin resistance with an inadequate beta-cell response.
cards.ex: One is a supply failure; the other is a resistance problem with relative deficiency.

cards.f: Why does hyperglycaemia cause polyuria?
cards.b: Glucose above the renal threshold is not fully reabsorbed, so it remains in the tubule and holds water (osmotic diuresis).
cards.ex: Unabsorbed solute keeps water in the nephron.

cards.f: Why can plasma potassium be normal in DKA despite total body depletion?
cards.b: Acidosis and lack of insulin move potassium out of cells, offsetting urinary losses; insulin treatment drives potassium back into cells and plasma levels can fall quickly.
cards.ex: Only about 2% of body potassium is in the extracellular fluid.

cards.f: Asymptomatic, single HbA1c 50 mmol/mol: what next?
cards.b: It is in the diabetic range, but without symptoms the result should be confirmed with a repeat test before diagnosing.
cards.ex: A single abnormal result may be a laboratory or biological variation.

cards.f: Why can an SGLT2 inhibitor cause DKA with glucose only 9 mmol/L?
cards.b: Glycosuria lowers glucose independent of insulin while insulin deficiency still drives ketogenesis, so ketoacidosis can occur with near-normal glucose (euglycaemic DKA).
cards.ex: Glucose is no longer a reliable guide to ketone production.

cards.f: Body water compartments (70 kg adult man)
cards.b: Total body water about 42 L (60%): intracellular about 28 L (two-thirds), extracellular about 14 L (one-third), of which plasma is about 3–3.5 L (approximate).
cards.ex: Roughly a fifth to a quarter of the ECF is plasma; the rest is interstitial fluid.

cards.f: Estimated plasma osmolality
cards.b: 2 × [Na⁺] + [glucose] + [urea] (mmol/L); about 290 mOsm/kg for sodium 140, glucose 5 and urea 5.
cards.ex: Sodium and its anions are doubled to account for their accompanying anions.

cards.f: How does ADH make urine concentrated?
cards.b: ADH acts on collecting duct cells to insert aquaporin-2 channels, so water is reabsorbed down the medullary osmotic gradient.
cards.ex: Without aquaporins the collecting duct is largely impermeable to water.

cards.f: Why is urea an ineffective osmole?
cards.b: It crosses cell membranes freely, so it does not create a lasting osmotic gradient or hold water in the ECF.
cards.ex: Only solutes that cannot cross the membrane make water move.

cards.f: Effective versus ineffective osmoles
cards.b: Effective (tonicity): sodium and its anions, glucose when insulin is lacking. Ineffective: urea and other solutes that cross membranes freely.
cards.ex: Tonicity depends on solutes that stay on one side.

cards.f: Why does hyponatraemia usually mean too much water rather than too little sodium?
cards.b: Plasma sodium is a concentration, so it falls when water is retained relative to sodium; total body sodium may be normal, low or high.
