cards.ex: A concentration changes with the denominator (water).

cards.f: Na 122, glucose 5.0, urea 3.1: calculated osmolality?
cards.b: 2 × 122 + 5.0 + 3.1 = 252.1 mOsm/kg, low, consistent with hypotonic hyponatraemia; a low measured osmolality confirms it, because in pseudohyponatraemia the calculated value is low but the measured value is normal.
cards.ex: Compare with the typical 285–295 range.

cards.f: Why does nephrotic syndrome cause oedema?
cards.b: Urinary albumin loss lowers plasma oncotic pressure, so net capillary filtration rises and fluid collects in the tissues; renal sodium retention also contributes.
cards.ex: Starling forces: oncotic pressure normally retains fluid in capillaries.

cards.f: Sequence of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system
cards.b: Fall in renal perfusion → renin from juxtaglomerular cells → angiotensin II (vasoconstriction, thirst) → aldosterone → sodium and water retention and potassium loss.
cards.ex: The system defends volume and blood pressure.

cards.f: Which hormone opposes aldosterone's effect on sodium?
cards.b: Atrial natriuretic peptide, released by atrial stretch, promotes sodium excretion.
cards.ex: It is the volume-overload counterpart of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

cards.f: Control of water balance versus sodium balance
cards.b: Water balance (osmolality): osmoreceptors, ADH, thirst. Sodium balance (ECF volume): renin–angiotensin–aldosterone, ANP, sympathetic activity.
cards.ex: Different sensors and effectors handle concentration and content.

cards.f: How does aldosterone raise sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion?
cards.b: It increases sodium channels and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in distal tubule and collecting duct principal cells; sodium entry makes the lumen negative, favouring potassium secretion.
cards.ex: Sodium moving in is balanced by potassium moving out.

cards.f: Why is hyperkalaemia dangerous to the heart?
cards.b: Raised extracellular potassium partially depolarises cardiac cells, so they cannot repolarise properly; conduction slows and fatal arrhythmias can follow.
cards.ex: A less negative resting potential inactivates sodium channels.

cards.f: Why does insulin lower plasma potassium?
cards.b: Insulin stimulates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and drives potassium into cells, shifting it from plasma without removing it from the body.
cards.ex: It is a redistribution, not an excretion.

cards.f: Potassium 6.8 mmol/L with peaked T waves: how serious?
cards.b: It is a dangerous hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, an emergency needing urgent assessment and treatment.
cards.ex: ECG changes show the myocardium is already affected.

cards.f: A 78-year-old is nil by mouth after surgery, with no signs of hypovolaemia and a normal U&E. Following NICE CG174, how should routine maintenance IV fluids be approached?
cards.b: Use IV fluids only if oral or enteral routes cannot meet needs; start with a restricted prescription of water, electrolytes (including potassium) and glucose, consider less for older or frail patients, and reassess clinical status, U&E and fluid balance at least daily.
cards.ex: The aim is to meet needs without causing fluid overload.

cards.f: Net filtration pressure in the glomerulus
cards.b: Glomerular hydrostatic 55 − (capsular hydrostatic 15 + oncotic 30) = 10 mmHg (approximate values).
cards.ex: Only the hydrostatic pressure favours filtration.

cards.f: NG148 criteria for AKI (any one)
cards.b: Creatinine rise of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours; a rise of 50% or more known or presumed to have occurred within the past 7 days; urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours.
cards.ex: Absolute rise, relative rise or urine output.

cards.f: How does tubuloglomerular feedback work?
cards.b: The macula densa senses sodium chloride delivery; if it is high (GFR too high) the afferent arteriole constricts and GFR falls, and if it is low renin is released and the afferent arteriole dilates.
cards.ex: It adjusts GFR to match what the tubule can reabsorb.

cards.f: Why can NSAIDs plus ACE inhibitors plus a diuretic cause AKI?
cards.b: NSAIDs remove prostaglandin dilation of the afferent arteriole, ACE inhibitors remove efferent constriction, and the diuretic reduces volume, so glomerular pressure and GFR fall.
cards.ex: Autoregulation depends on both arterioles.

cards.f: Calculate clearance: U 6 mmol/L, V 2 mL/min, P 0.1 mmol/L
cards.ex: Divide the excretion rate by the plasma concentration.

cards.f: AKI versus CKD
cards.b: AKI: rapid rise in creatinine or fall in urine output over hours to days (NG148). CKD: abnormal kidney structure or function for more than 3 months, graded by GFR and ACR (NG203).
cards.ex: The time course separates them.

cards.f: Creatinine 190 µmol/L, baseline 84: UKKA stage?
cards.b: 190 ÷ 84 = 2.26 times baseline, which is stage 2 (2.0–2.9 times).
cards.ex: Use the ratio to baseline.

cards.f: Why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate GFR?
cards.b: A small amount of creatinine is secreted by the proximal tubule in addition to being filtered.
cards.ex: Added secretion makes more appear in urine than was filtered.

cards.f: Henderson–Hasselbalch equation (CO₂ in kPa)
cards.b: pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻] ÷ (0.225 × PaCO₂)).
cards.ex: A ratio of about 20:1 gives a pH near 7.4.

cards.f: Anion gap
cards.b: Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); typical range roughly 8–16 mmol/L, varying by laboratory.
cards.ex: Raised gap means unmeasured anions such as lactate or ketones.

cards.f: How does the kidney create new bicarbonate?
cards.b: Collecting duct cells secrete H⁺, which is buffered in the urine by phosphate and ammonia; for each H⁺ excreted this way a new bicarbonate enters the blood.
cards.ex: Acid excretion and bicarbonate generation are linked.

cards.f: Metabolic versus respiratory acidosis
cards.b: Metabolic: low bicarbonate, compensation by lowering PaCO₂. Respiratory: high PaCO₂, compensation by renal bicarbonate retention over days.
cards.ex: Check which of the two moves in the direction that explains the pH.

cards.f: Why does vomiting cause a metabolic alkalosis?
cards.b: It loses gastric hydrochloric acid, so H⁺ is lost and bicarbonate is left in excess; volume contraction and potassium loss help maintain it.
cards.ex: The loss is of acid, not of bicarbonate.

cards.f: Winter's formula for bicarbonate 18
cards.b: Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × 18 + 8 = 35 mmHg ± 2, which is 33–37 mmHg or about 4.4–4.9 kPa.
cards.ex: Divide mmHg by 7.5 for kPa.

cards.f: pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 8.6 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 32
cards.b: Respiratory acidosis (high PaCO₂ explains the low pH) with a raised bicarbonate showing renal compensation over days.
cards.ex: Chronic CO₂ retention, as in COPD.

cards.f: Why does a normal pH not exclude acid–base disease?
cards.b: Opposing disorders or compensation can pull pH back to near normal; the PaCO₂ and bicarbonate still reveal the abnormality.
cards.ex: Interpret all three values together.

questions.q: Which of the following abdominal structures is retroperitoneal?
questions.why: The ascending and descending colon, most of the duodenum, the pancreas and the rectum are retroperitoneal. Organs on a mesentery or omentum are intraperitoneal.
optWhy: It hangs from the transverse mesocolon, so it is intraperitoneal and mobile.
Correct: the ascending colon lies behind the peritoneum, fixed to the posterior abdominal wall.
It is suspended by the small-bowel mesentery and is intraperitoneal.
It is intraperitoneal, slung from the lesser and greater omenta.
questions.clue: Which structure lies behind the peritoneum?
questions.concept: Retroperitoneal versus intraperitoneal organs.

followUp.q: Inflammation of which organ often causes pain that bores through to the back because the organ lies behind the peritoneum?
followUp.why: The pancreas is retroperitoneal, so pain from pancreatic inflammation is classically felt in the epigastrium and radiates to the back. The ileum and sigmoid colon are on mesenteries and the spleen is intraperitoneal.

questions.q: A 72-year-old has colicky central abdominal pain, vomiting and distension. An abdominal radiograph shows centrally placed dilated bowel loops up to 4.5 cm wide with folds crossing the full width of the lumen, and no gas in the rectum. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Normal small-bowel calibre, because small bowel can be up to 6 cm
Large-bowel obstruction, because the bowel is dilated
Dilated small bowel, consistent with small-bowel obstruction
questions.why: The width of 4.5 cm exceeds the roughly 3 cm limit for small bowel, valvulae conniventes cross the whole lumen, and the absence of gas in the rectum suggests the obstruction is blocking onward gas. Together with colicky pain and vomiting this fits small-bowel obstruction.
optWhy: The 6 cm limit applies to the colon, not the small bowel, whose upper limit is about 3 cm.
Large bowel lies peripherally with haustra that do not cross the lumen and a 6 cm limit; central loops with full-width folds point to small bowel.
Correct: small bowel wider than about 3 cm with valvulae conniventes crossing the lumen and no distal gas fits small-bowel obstruction.
Perforation shows free gas under the diaphragm or Rigler's sign, not a pattern of dilated central loops.
questions.clue: Loops up to 4.5 cm wide with folds crossing the full width and no rectal gas.
questions.concept: Bowel calibre (3/6/9 rule) and valvulae conniventes identify dilated small bowel.

followUp.q: On an abdominal radiograph the caecum measures 11 cm and loops of colon at the periphery measure 7 cm with haustra visible. What does this suggest?
followUp.why: The colon limit is about 6 cm and the caecal limit about 9 cm, so both are exceeded and the peripheral haustral pattern identifies large bowel. This is not normal, small bowel is not the main problem, and free gas would appear under the diaphragm on an erect chest film.

questions.q: A 2-year-old has painless, large-volume rectal bleeding. Investigation finds a blind-ending pouch on the antimesenteric border of the ileum, about 60 cm from the ileocaecal valve, containing ectopic gastric mucosa. Which embryological structure failed to regress?
questions.why: The vitelline duct connects the midgut to the yolk sac and normally disappears. A persistent portion forms Meckel's diverticulum, classically about 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve and sometimes lined by gastric mucosa, whose acid can ulcerate neighbouring ileum and cause painless bleeding.
optWhy: A persistent urachus joins the bladder to the umbilicus and presents with urine leaking from the umbilicus.
Abnormal rotation of the ventral bud causes annular pancreas, which obstructs the duodenum.
Notochord remnants relate to the vertebral column and nucleus pulposus, not the ileum.
Correct: persistence of part of the vitelline duct gives Meckel's diverticulum, which can contain ectopic gastric mucosa.
questions.clue: Blind ileal pouch with ectopic gastric mucosa about 60 cm from the ileocaecal valve.
questions.concept: Meckel's diverticulum is a vitelline duct remnant.

followUp.q: Which embryonic structure's incomplete regression causes Meckel's diverticulum?
options: The allantoic stalk's connection to the cloaca
followUp.why: The vitelline duct links the midgut to the yolk sac. The urachus (from the allantois) links bladder and umbilicus, and the ductus venosus is a fetal liver bypass vessel.

questions.q: A 76-year-old with atrial fibrillation not taking anticoagulation develops sudden severe central abdominal pain, with an abdomen that is soft and not very tender. Embolic occlusion of which artery is most likely?
questions.why: Emboli from the fibrillating atrium often lodge in the superior mesenteric artery. Midgut ischaemia causes severe central or periumbilical pain that seems out of proportion to the examination findings early on.
optWhy: It supplies the hindgut and pain would be lower; its territory also has collateral supply from the marginal artery.
Correct: the superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut and is the commonest site of embolic mesenteric ischaemia.
It supplies the foregut and pain would be epigastric; rich collaterals protect against isolated occlusion.
It supplies pelvic structures, not the small bowel.
questions.clue: Atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation, sudden severe central pain with a soft abdomen.
questions.concept: Match the artery to its embryological territory and referred pain.

followUp.q: Which artery supplies the sigmoid colon?
options: Middle colic artery from the coeliac trunk
followUp.why: The sigmoid colon is hindgut and is supplied by branches of the inferior mesenteric artery. The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut and the coeliac trunk the foregut, and the middle colic artery is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery (not the coeliac trunk) that supplies the transverse colon.

questions.q: Describe the layers of the small-intestinal wall and explain how its structure is adapted for absorption.
markScheme: Four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa
Mucosa: simple columnar epithelium with microvilli (brush border), lamina propria and muscularis mucosae
Circular folds, villi and microvilli multiply the surface area (about 200 m², approximate)
Each villus has a capillary network and a lacteal for absorbed nutrients and fat
Plexuses: submucosal (secretion) and myenteric (motility); Brunner's glands in the duodenum or Peyer's patches in the ileum as examples of regional specialisation
questions.modelAnswer: From the lumen outwards the wall has four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa and serosa. The mucosa is lined by simple columnar epithelium whose apical microvilli form the brush border, with a lamina propria beneath and a thin muscularis mucosae. Circular folds, villi and microvilli together multiply the surface area to roughly 200 m² (approximate), maximising contact with chyme. Each villus contains a capillary network that carries absorbed sugars and amino acids to the portal blood, and a central lacteal that takes up chylomicrons into lymph. The submucosa carries the Meissner plexus controlling secretion and, in the duodenum, Brunner's glands secreting alkaline mucus; the muscularis externa has circular and longitudinal muscle with the Auerbach plexus controlling motility, producing segmentation and peristalsis. The ileum also contains Peyer's patches of lymphoid tissue.
questions.concept: Wall layers and villous structure.

questions.q: Which hormone is released from the duodenum when fat and protein arrive and stimulates both enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction?
questions.why: CCK links the arrival of fat and protein in the duodenum to the secretions needed to digest them: pancreatic enzymes and bile released by gallbladder contraction.
optWhy: It is released by stomach G cells and stimulates gastric acid secretion.
It responds to acid in the duodenum and stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice, not enzymes.
It is an endocrine pancreatic hormone controlling blood glucose, not a gut hormone controlling digestive secretions.
Correct: CCK is released in response to fat and protein and drives pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.
questions.clue: Fat and protein arrive in the duodenum; enzyme-rich juice plus gallbladder contraction.
questions.concept: CCK coordinates pancreatic enzymes and bile with the arrival of fat and protein.

followUp.q: Which hormone is released when acidic chyme enters the duodenum and mainly stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice?
followUp.why: Secretin responds to acid and neutralises it. CCK responds to fat and protein, gastrin acts on gastric acid and glucagon controls blood glucose.

questions.q: A 2-year-old has several days of watery diarrhoea and is mildly dehydrated but drinking. Why is an oral rehydration solution that contains both glucose and sodium effective even though the diarrhoea is severe?
options: Glucose stimulates ADH release, which makes the gut absorb water
Sodium-coupled glucose cotransport in the small intestine remains active and water follows the absorbed solute
Glucose blocks the chloride secretion that causes the diarrhoea
Glucose acts as an osmotic laxative that flushes toxins out of the gut
questions.why: Even in secretory diarrhoea the SGLT1 cotransporter continues to work. Absorbing sodium and glucose together creates an osmotic gradient that draws water across the epithelium, so losses can be replaced by mouth.
optWhy: Glucose does not block chloride secretion; it works by driving sodium and water absorption through a separate pathway.
Excess unabsorbed glucose would worsen osmotic diarrhoea; the solution is balanced so glucose is absorbed.
ADH acts on the kidney collecting duct to conserve water; it does not make the intestine absorb water.
Correct: SGLT1 still moves sodium and glucose into enterocytes together, and water is absorbed with them.
questions.clue: Severe diarrhoea but mildly dehydrated and drinking; solution contains both glucose and sodium.
questions.concept: Sodium-coupled glucose absorption is preserved in diarrhoea and drives water uptake.

followUp.q: Which transport process explains why adding glucose to a sodium-containing drink speeds up sodium and water uptake from the small intestine?
options: Passive diffusion of sodium through tight junctions only
Active secretion of sodium into the lumen
followUp.why: Glucose and sodium enter the enterocyte on the same carrier, so the two are absorbed together and water follows. Chloride secretion and sodium secretion into the lumen would increase fluid loss, and diffusion through tight junctions alone is far less effective.

questions.q: A 60-year-old who had a long section of terminal ileum removed for Crohn's disease has a haemoglobin of 98 g/L and an MCV of 112 fL. Which absorptive failure best explains this?
options: Failure to digest lactose because of loss of brush-border lactase
Failure to absorb iron in the terminal ileum
Failure to absorb vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor in the terminal ileum
Failure to secrete intrinsic factor from the stomach
questions.why: The gastric parietal cells still make intrinsic factor, but the terminal ileum is where the B12–intrinsic factor complex is absorbed. B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, giving enlarged red cells (high MCV) and anaemia.
optWhy: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, and iron deficiency causes a low MCV, not a high one.
Correct: this complex is taken up in the terminal ileum, so resection causes B12 deficiency and a macrocytic anaemia.
Intrinsic factor is made by gastric parietal cells, which are unaffected by ileal resection.
Lactose intolerance gives bloating and diarrhoea, not macrocytic anaemia.
questions.clue: Terminal ileal resection, haemoglobin 98 g/L, MCV 112 fL.
questions.concept: The terminal ileum is the site of B12 absorption.

followUp.q: A strict vegan with a normal ileum and stomach develops macrocytic anaemia. What is the most likely cause?
followUp.why: B12 comes almost entirely from animal products or fortified foods, so a diet without them can cause deficiency. Intrinsic factor loss and ileal disease are absorption problems, and lipase deficiency causes fat malabsorption.

questions.q: A 55-year-old with long-standing alcohol-related chronic pancreatitis has weight loss and pale, bulky, foul-smelling stools that float. Which deficiency is the main cause of the stool change?
options: Reduced pancreatic amylase, so starch is not digested
Reduced pancreatic lipase, so dietary fat is not digested or absorbed
Reduced intrinsic factor, so vitamin B12 is not absorbed
Reduced gastrin, so acid secretion is low
questions.why: Pancreatic lipase is the main enzyme digesting triglycerides, and chronic pancreatitis also reduces bicarbonate that keeps the duodenum at a pH where lipase works. Undigested fat in the stool makes it pale, bulky and buoyant, and fat-soluble vitamins may also become deficient.
optWhy: Salivary amylase and brush-border carbohydrases compensate; carbohydrate malabsorption causes osmotic, watery diarrhoea and gas rather than fatty stools.
Correct: lack of lipase causes fat maldigestion and steatorrhoea.
This causes a macrocytic anaemia and neurological problems, not fatty stool.
Low acid affects protein digestion and B12 release from food but does not cause steatorrhoea.
questions.clue: Chronic pancreatitis, pale bulky foul stools that float.
questions.concept: Steatorrhoea results from lipase deficiency or lack of bile salts.

followUp.q: Which finding would most strongly support pancreatic exocrine insufficiency in a person with steatorrhoea?
followUp.why: Faecal elastase is a pancreatic enzyme that survives gut transit, so a low level shows reduced exocrine output. A high level argues against insufficiency, and ferritin or B12 do not test pancreatic function.

questions.q: Describe how a meal containing starch, protein and fat is digested and absorbed in the small intestine. Include the roles of bile and the pancreas.
markScheme: Starch: pancreatic (and salivary) amylase then brush-border enzymes give glucose, galactose, fructose; sodium-coupled absorption of glucose and galactose, facilitated diffusion of fructose
Protein: pepsin then pancreatic proteases (zymogens activated by enteropeptidase) and brush-border peptidases give amino acids and small peptides
Fat: bile salts emulsify; pancreatic lipase gives fatty acids and monoglycerides; micelles carry them to the brush border
Enterocytes rebuild triglycerides into chylomicrons that enter lacteals and lymph
Pancreatic bicarbonate neutralises acid chyme; CCK and secretin coordinate pancreatic and biliary secretion; most absorption is in duodenum and jejunum
questions.modelAnswer: Starch is partly broken down by salivary amylase and then by pancreatic amylase, and brush-border enzymes such as maltase and sucrase produce glucose, galactose and fructose. Glucose and galactose are absorbed on a sodium-coupled transporter and fructose by facilitated diffusion. Proteins are cleaved by pepsin in the stomach and then by pancreatic proteases, which are secreted as inactive zymogens and activated by enteropeptidase, and brush-border peptidases leave amino acids, dipeptides and tripeptides that are absorbed in the duodenum and jejunum. Fat needs bile: bile salts emulsify it so pancreatic lipase can produce fatty acids and monoglycerides, which are carried in micelles to the brush border, absorbed, rebuilt into triglycerides and packaged into chylomicrons that enter lacteals. The pancreas also secretes bicarbonate that neutralises the acid chyme so enzymes work at a suitable pH. CCK (from fat and protein) and secretin (from acid) coordinate the pancreatic and biliary response.
questions.concept: Digestion and absorption of the three macronutrients.

questions.q: Which form of bilirubin is water-soluble and can appear in the urine?
questions.why: Only conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble. In obstructive jaundice it regurgitates into the blood and is filtered, darkening the urine.
optWhy: It is lipid-soluble and protein-bound, so it is not filtered by the glomerulus.
Correct: conjugation with glucuronic acid makes bilirubin water-soluble so it can be excreted in bile or, when bile is blocked, filtered into urine.
This is the green pigment formed from haem before reduction to bilirubin; it is not the form measured as conjugated bilirubin.
This is the brown stool pigment made by gut bacteria from bilirubin, not a form of bilirubin in blood.
questions.clue: Which form of bilirubin can appear in urine?
questions.concept: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble; unconjugated is albumin-bound.

followUp.q: A patient has jaundice from a haemolytic anaemia. What would be expected of the urine bilirubin and why?
options: Strongly positive, because all bilirubin is filtered
Absent, because the raised unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not filtered
Absent, because the liver is damaged
Strongly positive, because red cell breakdown releases conjugated bilirubin directly
followUp.why: Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, which is albumin-bound and not filtered, so urine bilirubin is absent (acholuric jaundice). Not all bilirubin is filtered, the liver is usually healthy, and red cells release haem that is conjugated only in hepatocytes.

questions.q: A 22-year-old student has noticed yellow eyes while fasting during a viral illness. Bilirubin is 38 µmol/L, almost all unconjugated; ALT, ALP and haemoglobin are normal and there is no evidence of haemolysis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Obstruction of the common bile duct by a gallstone
questions.why: Gilbert's syndrome reduces glucuronyl transferase activity modestly. Bilirubin rises during fasting or intercurrent illness, ALT and ALP stay normal, and the condition is harmless, so reassurance is appropriate.
optWhy: Correct: mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with otherwise normal liver tests and no haemolysis, brought out by fasting or illness.
Obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin and ALP and GGT, and causes dark urine and pale stools.
This would produce a markedly raised ALT and often a mixed bilirubin rise.
Haemolysis would reduce haemoglobin and show haemolysis markers; here haemoglobin is normal.
questions.clue: Fasting during illness, mostly unconjugated bilirubin, normal ALT, ALP and haemoglobin.
questions.concept: Gilbert's syndrome is isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without haemolysis or liver disease.

followUp.q: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is found in a patient with falling haemoglobin and a raised reticulocyte count. What is the most likely cause?
followUp.why: Falling haemoglobin with raised reticulocytes shows red cells are being destroyed faster than made. Gilbert's syndrome does not lower haemoglobin, a bile duct stone raises conjugated bilirubin and cholestatic enzymes, and alcohol-related hepatitis raises aminotransferases.

questions.q: A 48-year-old has itching and has noticed dark urine and pale stools. Bilirubin is 70 µmol/L (mostly conjugated), ALP 540 U/L, GGT 420 U/L, ALT 85 U/L. Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: A bone scan, because ALP is raised
Repeat the blood tests in one year, because ALT is only mildly raised
Reticulocyte count and haptoglobin to look for haemolysis
Abdominal ultrasound to look for bile duct dilatation or stones
questions.why: ALP and GGT are raised far more than ALT, with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, dark urine, pale stools and itch: cholestasis. Ultrasound is the usual first test to show dilated ducts and stones.
optWhy: Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and does not raise ALP or GGT.
Correct: a cholestatic pattern needs imaging to find a mechanical obstruction.
The raised GGT shows the ALP is hepatic or biliary, not bony.
Dark urine, pale stools and a high ALP with GGT suggest obstruction that should be investigated promptly.
questions.clue: Dark urine, pale stools, mostly conjugated bilirubin, ALP 540 and GGT 420 with ALT 85.
questions.concept: A cholestatic pattern calls for imaging of the biliary tree.

followUp.q: A raised ALP is found with a normal GGT in a man with bone pain. What does this suggest?
options: Obstruction of the common bile duct
The ALP probably comes from bone
followUp.why: GGT is not present in bone, so a normal GGT with a raised ALP points away from the liver. Bile duct obstruction and alcohol-related disease usually raise GGT, and acute hepatitis raises ALT and AST much more than ALP.

questions.q: A 52-year-old with heavy alcohol intake has AST 168 U/L, ALT 70 U/L, GGT 410 U/L, MCV 106 fL and a low platelet count. What is the AST:ALT ratio and what does the overall picture suggest?
options: About 2.4; alcohol-related liver injury with possible advanced fibrosis
About 2.4; obstructive jaundice from a bile duct stone
questions.why: AST:ALT is 168 ÷ 70 = 2.4. A ratio above 1 raises concern for advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis (BSG guideline), and the low platelet count adds to that concern; heavy drinking with a raised GGT and a high MCV points to alcohol as the cause.
optWhy: Correct: 168 ÷ 70 = 2.4, a ratio above 1 that suggests advanced fibrosis, and heavy drinking with a raised GGT and macrocytosis points to alcohol-related liver injury.
0.4 is 70 ÷ 168, the inverse ratio; viral hepatitis usually has ALT higher than AST.
Obstruction raises ALP and GGT with bilirubin, not a predominantly raised AST with macrocytosis.
The ratio is not 1.0, and the GGT, MCV and platelets are all abnormal.
questions.clue: AST 168 and ALT 70 with GGT 410, MCV 106 and low platelets in a heavy drinker.
questions.concept: AST:ALT ratio and associated findings help to identify alcohol-related disease and fibrosis.

followUp.q: A patient has ALT 1,100 U/L, AST 900 U/L and ALP 130 U/L (all other results normal). Which pattern is this?
followUp.why: Aminotransferases are raised far more than ALP, which is the hepatitic pattern. A cholestatic pattern has ALP and GGT raised most, and the other options do not describe these results.

questions.q: Describe the metabolism of bilirubin and explain how the findings differ between pre-hepatic and obstructive jaundice.
markScheme: Haem from red cells is converted to biliverdin then unconjugated bilirubin, carried on albumin
Hepatocytes take it up and conjugate it with glucuronic acid, giving water-soluble conjugated bilirubin that is secreted into bile
Gut bacteria convert it to urobilinogen and stercobilin, colouring stool brown
Pre-hepatic: excess unconjugated bilirubin, normal urine and stool colour (not filtered)
Obstructive: raised conjugated bilirubin, dark urine, pale stool, itch, raised ALP and GGT
questions.modelAnswer: Haem released when ageing red cells are broken down is converted to biliverdin and then to unconjugated bilirubin, which is lipid-soluble and travels bound to albumin. Hepatocytes take it up and conjugate it with glucuronic acid, making it water-soluble, and secrete it into bile. In the gut, bacteria convert it to urobilinogen and then stercobilin, which colours the stool brown; a little urobilinogen is reabsorbed and excreted in urine. In pre-hepatic jaundice, for example haemolysis, the supply of bilirubin exceeds the liver's capacity to conjugate it, so unconjugated bilirubin rises; it is albumin-bound and not filtered, so the urine is a normal colour and the stool is normal. In obstructive jaundice, bile cannot reach the gut, so conjugated bilirubin regurgitates into the blood and is filtered, making the urine dark, while the stool is pale because little bilirubin reaches the gut. Retained bile salts cause itch, and ALP and GGT are raised.
questions.concept: Bilirubin metabolism and the types of jaundice.

questions.q: What is the UK recommended maximum for free sugars as a proportion of adult energy intake?
questions.why: UK advice is that free sugars should provide no more than 5% of energy. They are added sugars plus sugars in honey, syrups and fruit juices, not the sugars inside intact fruit.
optWhy: This was the earlier recommendation before it was lowered to 5%.
This is far above any UK target.
Correct: the Government Dietary Recommendations and current GOV.UK guidance give no more than 5% of energy from free sugars.
This is far above any UK free sugars target.
questions.clue: UK maximum for free sugars as a share of energy.
questions.concept: UK dietary targets for free sugars.

followUp.q: An adult eats 2,000 kcal a day. At the 5% free sugars limit, roughly how many grams of free sugars is that (4 kcal per gram)?
followUp.why: 5% of 2,000 kcal is 100 kcal; dividing by 4 kcal per gram gives 25 g. 50 g corresponds to the older 10% limit, 100 g reads the 100 kcal as grams, and 11 g divides by 9 kcal per gram, the energy density of fat.

questions.q: A man weighs 82 kg and is 1.75 m tall. What is his BMI and category?
questions.why: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². Squaring 1.75 gives 3.0625, and 82 ÷ 3.0625 = 26.8, which is in the overweight band (25–29.9).
optWhy: 46.9 is 82 ÷ 1.75, which forgets to square the height.
Correct: 82 ÷ 1.75² = 82 ÷ 3.0625 = 26.8, which falls in the 25–29.9 overweight range.
23.4 is 82 ÷ (2 × 1.75), which doubles the height instead of squaring it.
0.037 is 1.75² ÷ 82, inverting the formula.
questions.clue: Weight 82 kg and height 1.75 m.
questions.concept: BMI = weight ÷ height² and its categories.

followUp.q: A woman weighs 95 kg and is 1.70 m tall. What is her BMI and category?
followUp.why: 95 ÷ 1.70² = 95 ÷ 2.89 = 32.9, in the obesity range (30 or above). 55.9 forgets to square the height, 27.9 doubles the height, and 32.9 is not in the overweight band.

questions.q: A 58 kg, 1.62 m tall patient admitted with severe pneumonia had weighed 65 kg three months ago and is expected to eat nothing for more than 5 days. What is the MUST score and risk category?
questions.why: BMI = 58 ÷ 1.62² = 22.1 (score 0). Weight loss = (65 − 58) ÷ 65 = 10.8%, which is above 10% (score 2). Acute disease effect with no intake expected for more than 5 days scores 2. Total 4, high risk (2 or more).
optWhy: This omits the acute disease effect score of 2 that applies when no intake is expected for more than 5 days.
This scores the weight loss as 1, as if it were 5–10%; 10.8% is just above 10% and scores 2.
Correct: BMI 22.1 scores 0, weight loss 10.8% scores 2, acute disease effect scores 2: total 4.
This wrongly adds a BMI score of 2, but BMI 22.1 is above 20 and scores 0.
questions.clue: Weight 58 kg, height 1.62 m, previous 65 kg, no intake for more than 5 days.
questions.concept: MUST scoring from BMI, weight loss and acute disease effect.

followUp.q: A patient has BMI 17.5 and 3% weight loss and is acutely ill with no intake expected for more than 5 days. What is the MUST score?
followUp.why: BMI below 18.5 scores 2, weight loss under 5% scores 0 and the acute disease effect scores 2: total 4. A score of 2 omits the acute effect, 0 ignores the BMI, and 1 matches no combination of the scores.

questions.q: A 54-year-old man with alcohol dependence and poor diet is brought in confused, with unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements. Which deficiency is most likely, and what is the key principle before giving glucose?
options: Thiamine deficiency; replace thiamine before or with glucose
Vitamin C deficiency; give glucose first to correct hypoglycaemia
Vitamin B12 deficiency; give glucose first
Niacin deficiency; avoid all vitamins until the confusion settles
questions.why: Confusion, ataxia and abnormal eye movements in alcohol dependence make Wernicke's encephalopathy likely. Thiamine is a cofactor for glucose metabolism and stores are low, so giving glucose alone can use up what is left; thiamine is given before or with glucose (doses are not given here). If hypoglycaemia is present, it is treated without delay and thiamine is given as soon as possible.
optWhy: Scurvy causes bleeding gums, bruising and poor healing, not confusion, ataxia and eye-movement problems; and in a person at risk, glucose is not given ahead of thiamine unless hypoglycaemia needs immediate treatment.
B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia and neuropathy or subacute combined degeneration, not acute confusion with ophthalmoplegia.
Pellagra causes dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia, and vitamins are not withheld.
Correct: Wernicke's encephalopathy is caused by thiamine deficiency, and a glucose load can worsen it.
questions.clue: Alcohol dependence with confusion, unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements.
questions.concept: Wernicke's encephalopathy is thiamine deficiency; thiamine accompanies glucose in at-risk people.

followUp.q: A severely underweight patient who has eaten almost nothing for 12 days is about to start artificial nutrition. Which biochemical change is the main refeeding danger?
options: A fall in plasma phosphate, potassium and magnesium
A rise in plasma sodium only
A fall in plasma calcium only
followUp.why: Insulin released on refeeding drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, so plasma levels drop and can cause arrhythmias and weakness. Plasma phosphate does not rise, and sodium or calcium alone do not describe refeeding syndrome.

questions.q: A 74-year-old woman is 1.60 m tall, weighs 56 kg and has lost 8 kg over four months. She is not acutely ill. Calculate her BMI and percentage weight loss, score her MUST and state what the result means.
markScheme: BMI = 56 ÷ 1.60² = 21.9 kg/m², score 0
Percentage weight loss = 8 ÷ 64 × 100 = 12.5%, score 2 (above 10%)
Acute disease effect score 0, since she is not acutely ill
Total 2 = high risk of malnutrition
Treat: dietitian or nutrition support, set goals and care plan, treat the underlying cause; a normal BMI can hide significant weight loss
questions.modelAnswer: Her previous weight was 56 + 8 = 64 kg. BMI = 56 ÷ (1.60 × 1.60) = 56 ÷ 2.56 = 21.9 kg/m², which is above 20 and scores 0. Percentage weight loss = 8 ÷ 64 × 100 = 12.5%, which is above 10% and scores 2. She is not acutely ill, so the acute disease score is 0. The total is 2, which is high risk of malnutrition on MUST. This should lead to treatment: referral to a dietitian or nutrition support team, setting goals, a care plan, and finding and treating the cause of the weight loss. It shows that a normal BMI can hide serious malnutrition, which is why unplanned weight loss is scored.
questions.concept: MUST scoring and interpretation.

questions.q: Which of the following cannot be converted to glucose by gluconeogenesis in humans?
questions.why: Gluconeogenesis uses lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids. Fatty acids give acetyl-CoA, which enters the citric acid cycle or ketone synthesis but cannot make net glucose.
optWhy: Lactate from anaerobic metabolism is converted to pyruvate and then to glucose in the liver (the Cori cycle).
Glycerol from triglyceride breakdown enters gluconeogenesis.
Correct: they are broken down to acetyl-CoA, which cannot be converted back to pyruvate.
This amino acid is a major gluconeogenic substrate released from muscle.
questions.clue: Which substrate cannot form glucose?
questions.concept: Fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose.

followUp.q: Which product of triglyceride breakdown can be used by the liver to make glucose?
followUp.why: The glycerol backbone is phosphorylated and enters gluconeogenesis. Palmitate is a fatty acid, acetyl-CoA derives from fatty acids, and acetoacetate is a ketone body; none can form net glucose.

questions.q: A healthy volunteer has not eaten for 10 hours. Which process is the main source of the glucose entering the blood?
options: Release of glucose from muscle glycogen
Absorption of glucose from the last meal
Conversion of ketone bodies to glucose
Glycogenolysis in the liver, with gluconeogenesis beginning
questions.why: After an overnight fast, falling insulin and rising glucagon activate hepatic glycogenolysis, and gluconeogenesis starts to contribute as liver glycogen falls.
optWhy: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so its glycogen cannot supply blood glucose directly.
By 10 hours digestion and absorption are complete, so intestinal absorption is no longer contributing.
Ketones cannot be converted to glucose; they serve as an alternative fuel.
Correct: liver glycogen is broken down first, then gluconeogenesis contributes more as the fast lengthens.
questions.clue: No food for 10 hours; source of blood glucose.
questions.concept: Hepatic glycogenolysis then gluconeogenesis maintains blood glucose in fasting.

followUp.q: Why can muscle glycogen not be used to raise blood glucose?
options: Muscle glycogen is a different molecule from liver glycogen
Insulin prevents muscle glycogen breakdown at all times
followUp.why: Muscle has phosphorylase and the same glycogen structure, but without glucose-6-phosphatase it cannot release free glucose. Insulin suppresses breakdown in the fed state only.

questions.q: A 24-year-old has been fasting for 4 days. Capillary glucose is 3.9 mmol/L, ketones are elevated and venous pH and bicarbonate are normal. A second patient has glucose 31 mmol/L, ketones above 5 mmol/L, pH 7.05 and bicarbonate 5 mmol/L. What best explains the difference between them?
options: Insulin is present in the first patient and restrains ketogenesis, but is absent in the second
The second patient has been fasting for longer
The first patient has a lower rate of fatty acid oxidation than the second
Ketone bodies are neutral compounds in the first patient but acids in the second
questions.why: In prolonged fasting a small amount of insulin remains and keeps lipolysis and ketogenesis within a range the buffers and kidneys can handle. In DKA insulin is almost absent, so lipolysis and ketogenesis are unrestrained and the acid load overwhelms buffers, lowering pH and bicarbonate.
optWhy: Both oxidise fat; the difference is how far insulin restrains lipolysis and ketogenesis.
Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are acids in both; the difference is the amount produced.
Correct: insulin limits lipolysis and ketone production, so ketosis in fasting does not reach the acidosis of DKA.
DKA does not need a longer fast; it results from absent insulin with high counter-regulatory hormones.
questions.clue: Normal pH and low-normal glucose after fasting versus glucose 31 with pH 7.05.
questions.concept: Insulin restrains ketogenesis; absence produces DKA.

followUp.q: Why does a person with type 1 diabetes who omits insulin develop ketoacidosis within hours, when a healthy person fasting does not?
options: Without insulin there is no restraint on lipolysis and ketogenesis
Healthy people do not produce ketones
Type 1 diabetes increases the liver's ability to metabolise ketones
The brain consumes all ketones in healthy people
followUp.why: Healthy people do produce ketones in fasting, but insulin keeps production moderate. In type 1 diabetes without insulin nothing limits lipolysis, and the liver cannot clear the ketone load, so acidosis follows.

questions.q: A 34-year-old in septic shock has cold peripheries, a lactate of 6.5 mmol/L, a bicarbonate of 14 mmol/L and a raised anion gap. Which metabolic change best explains the lactate?
options: Anaerobic glycolysis with pyruvate reduced to lactate in poorly perfused tissue
questions.why: When oxygen delivery fails, pyruvate cannot enter oxidative phosphorylation and is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺. Lactate accumulates and, being an unmeasured acid, consumes bicarbonate and raises the anion gap.
optWhy: This produces acetyl-CoA and ketone bodies, not lactate.
Correct: low oxygen delivery stops oxidative phosphorylation, so pyruvate is converted to lactate.
This causes hyperammonaemia, not lactic acidosis.
Gluconeogenesis consumes lactate; it does not generate it.
questions.clue: Septic shock, cold peripheries, lactate 6.5, raised anion gap.
questions.concept: Lactic acidosis arises from anaerobic glycolysis.

followUp.q: Why does a rise in lactate raise the anion gap?
options: Lactate is an unmeasured anion that replaces bicarbonate
Lactate is a cation that replaces chloride
Lactate lowers all measured anions equally
followUp.why: Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃). Lactate accumulates while bicarbonate is consumed, and because lactate is not measured the calculated gap rises. It is an anion, not a cation, and it does not raise sodium.

questions.q: Explain how blood glucose is maintained during an overnight fast and during several days of starvation.
markScheme: Overnight: falling insulin and rising glucagon activate hepatic glycogenolysis; liver glycogen lasts roughly a day
Gluconeogenesis in the liver from lactate, glycerol and amino acids contributes and increases as glycogen runs out
Lipolysis rises; most tissues use fatty acids, sparing glucose for brain and red cells
Prolonged fasting: hepatic ketogenesis produces ketone bodies that brain and heart use, reducing glucose need and protein breakdown
Muscle glycogen cannot supply blood glucose (no glucose-6-phosphatase); fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose
questions.modelAnswer: Overnight, as absorption ends, plasma glucose and insulin fall and glucagon rises. The liver breaks down glycogen (glycogenolysis) to release glucose, and starts gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and amino acids. Lipolysis increases, so muscle and other tissues switch to fatty acids and spare glucose for the brain and red blood cells. Liver glycogen lasts roughly a day (approximate). Muscle glycogen is not a source of blood glucose because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. Over several days of starvation hepatic glycogen is exhausted, and gluconeogenesis continues, mainly from glycerol, lactate and amino acids. Meanwhile the liver converts excess acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation into ketone bodies, which the brain and heart use as fuel. This reduces glucose requirement and therefore the breakdown of muscle protein for gluconeogenesis. Fatty acids themselves cannot be converted to glucose.
questions.concept: Fuel switching in fasting and starvation.

questions.q: What is the effect of insulin on adipose tissue?
options: It stimulates lipolysis to release fatty acids
It promotes triglyceride storage and suppresses lipolysis
questions.why: In the fed state insulin directs fuel into storage: glucose and fat are stored in adipose tissue and lipolysis is inhibited.
optWhy: Lipolysis is stimulated by fasting signals such as adrenaline when insulin is low; insulin suppresses it.
Correct: insulin stimulates storage and inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, restraining fatty acid release.
Ketogenesis occurs in the liver and is suppressed by insulin.
Insulin suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis.
questions.clue: Insulin's action in adipose tissue.
questions.concept: Insulin is anabolic and antilipolytic.

followUp.q: In the liver in the fed state, which pair of actions does insulin produce?
options: Promotes glycogen synthesis and suppresses gluconeogenesis
Suppresses glycogen synthesis and promotes lipolysis
followUp.why: Insulin drives storage and suppresses glucose output. The other pairs describe glucagon-like fasting effects or actions that insulin does not have.

questions.q: A 52-year-old attending a routine health check has no symptoms. HbA1c is 50 mmol/mol; haemoglobin and red cell indices are normal. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Diabetes can be diagnosed from this single result
The result is normal because it is below 53 mmol/mol
The result is in the diabetic range but should be confirmed with a repeat test
The result is in the prediabetes range of 42–47 mmol/mol
questions.why: The diagnostic cut-off is 48 mmol/mol, and 50 exceeds it. In an asymptomatic person a second test confirms the diagnosis; haemoglobin and indices are normal so HbA1c should be reliable.
optWhy: Without symptoms, UK guidance requires a repeat test to confirm.
53 mmol/mol is a treatment target for people on certain medicines, not the diagnostic threshold, which is 48.
Correct: without symptoms, a diabetic-range result requires confirmation.
50 is above 47 and so is in the diabetic range, not the high-risk range.
questions.clue: No symptoms, a single HbA1c of 50, normal haemoglobin and indices.
questions.concept: Diagnosis in asymptomatic people requires a confirmatory test.

followUp.q: A 30-year-old with thirst, polyuria and weight loss has a random plasma glucose of 14.2 mmol/L. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Diabetes can be diagnosed on this result
A repeat HbA1c in three months is required first
The result is in the high-risk (prediabetes) range
The result is normal for a random sample
followUp.why: A random glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or more with typical symptoms meets the diagnostic criteria. Waiting three months is not required, and 14.2 is not a high-risk or normal result.

questions.q: A 14-year-old has lost weight over several weeks and has polyuria, thirst and a glucose of 26 mmol/L. Which underlying mechanism is most likely?
options: Peripheral insulin resistance with preserved beta-cell function
Excess glucagon secretion by alpha cells with normal insulin
Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing absolute insulin deficiency
Renal glycosuria from a primary tubular defect
questions.why: Weight loss, polyuria and thirst over weeks with marked hyperglycaemia in a young person suggest autoimmune beta-cell destruction. Insulin is absent, so glucose is not taken up and lipolysis and ketogenesis are unrestrained.
optWhy: This would be a gradual process and is typical of type 2 diabetes with obesity, not rapid weight loss.
Glucagonoma is rare and does not typically present this way.
Correct: rapid onset in a young person with weight loss suggests type 1 diabetes.
This causes glycosuria with a normal blood glucose, not a glucose of 26 mmol/L.
questions.clue: Young age, weeks of weight loss, glucose 26 mmol/L.
questions.concept: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune absolute insulin deficiency.

followUp.q: Which feature favours type 2 rather than type 1 diabetes at presentation?
options: Gradual onset in an adult with central obesity
followUp.why: Type 2 develops gradually and is strongly linked to adiposity. The other features are more typical of type 1 diabetes.

questions.q: A 61-year-old with type 2 diabetes taking an SGLT2 inhibitor is vomiting with abdominal pain and rapid deep breathing. Glucose is 9.0 mmol/L, capillary ketones are 4.5 mmol/L, venous pH is 7.20 and bicarbonate is 12 mmol/L. How should this be interpreted?
options: Not DKA, because the glucose is below 11 mmol/L
questions.why: JBDS criteria require glucose above 11 mmol/L or known diabetes, ketones above 3.0 mmol/L and bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L and/or pH below 7.3. All three are met. SGLT2 inhibitors lower glucose through glycosuria, so ketoacidosis can occur with a modest glucose (euglycaemic DKA).
optWhy: The criteria are glucose above 11 mmol/L or known diabetes, so known diabetes satisfies that part.
Correct: known diabetes plus ketones above 3.0 mmol/L and pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15 fulfil the DKA criteria despite a modest glucose.
This needs a very high glucose with little ketosis and little acidosis.
Starvation ketosis keeps pH and bicarbonate near normal; here both are low.
questions.clue: Type 2 diabetes on an SGLT2 inhibitor; glucose 9.0, ketones 4.5, pH 7.20, bicarbonate 12.
questions.concept: DKA diagnosis depends on ketones and acidosis; euglycaemic DKA occurs with SGLT2 inhibitors.

followUp.q: Why do SGLT2 inhibitors lower blood glucose?
options: They block glucose absorption in the small intestine
They block glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule, causing glycosuria
They reduce hepatic glycogen breakdown by blocking glucagon receptors
followUp.why: SGLT2 is the main proximal tubular glucose transporter; blocking it makes the kidney excrete glucose. The other mechanisms belong to different drug classes or to no drug class.

questions.q: Using diabetic ketoacidosis as the example, explain how absolute insulin deficiency leads to hyperglycaemia, ketosis, dehydration and a disturbance of potassium balance.
markScheme: Without insulin, glucose uptake falls and the liver produces glucose by glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (with glucagon), so plasma glucose rises
Lipolysis is unrestrained; fatty acids go to the liver and become ketone bodies, which are acids, causing metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap
Glucose above the renal threshold causes osmotic diuresis, with loss of water and electrolytes and dehydration
Acidosis and lack of insulin move potassium out of cells; osmotic diuresis loses it, so total body potassium is low but plasma level may be normal or high
Respiratory compensation by deep breathing (Kussmaul); insulin treatment shifts potassium into cells so levels can fall
questions.modelAnswer: In absolute insulin deficiency, muscle and fat cannot take up glucose and the liver makes glucose through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, encouraged by glucagon, so plasma glucose rises. Lipolysis is also unrestrained, so large amounts of fatty acids reach the liver and are converted to ketone bodies (β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate). These are acids, so a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap develops, and the patient breathes deeply and rapidly to blow off carbon dioxide. When plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold, glycosuria produces an osmotic diuresis that causes dehydration and loss of sodium and potassium. Acidosis and absent insulin move potassium out of cells, so plasma potassium may be normal or high despite total body depletion; insulin treatment drives potassium back into cells and plasma potassium can fall quickly, which is why it is monitored and replaced.
questions.concept: Pathophysiology of DKA.

questions.q: Which solute is the main determinant of effective osmolality (tonicity) in the extracellular fluid?
questions.why: Sodium and its anions are confined largely to the ECF by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, so changes in their concentration move water across cell membranes.
optWhy: It crosses cell membranes freely, so it is an ineffective osmole.
It is the main intracellular cation; its extracellular concentration is small.
Its plasma concentration is small and it does not determine ECF tonicity.
Correct: sodium and its anions cannot cross cell membranes freely and hold water in the ECF.
questions.clue: Main determinant of ECF tonicity.
questions.concept: Sodium determines ECF tonicity.

followUp.q: Which solute is an ineffective osmole because it crosses cell membranes freely?
followUp.why: Urea equilibrates across cell membranes and does not hold water. Sodium and chloride are confined to the ECF, and glucose, in the absence of insulin, cannot enter many cells and so acts as an effective osmole.

questions.q: A 38-year-old finishes a marathon having drunk large volumes of plain water throughout. She is nauseated and confused, with a plasma sodium of 126 mmol/L. Which mechanism best explains the hyponatraemia?
options: Water intake exceeding excretion, with continued ADH release, diluting plasma sodium
Sodium lost in sweat with no water intake
questions.why: Hyponatraemia is a relative excess of water. Drinking more water than the kidney can excrete, with ADH still being released in response to non-osmotic stimuli, dilutes plasma sodium; sweat loss alone does not explain it.
optWhy: Correct: excess free water dilutes sodium, and non-osmotic stimuli such as nausea and stress maintain ADH.
Sweat loss without water replacement would raise sodium, not lower it.
Aldosterone retains sodium and would not cause a low plasma sodium.
This lowers measured sodium only when glucose is high; here there is no suggestion of hyperglycaemia.
questions.clue: Large volumes of plain water, sodium 126, nausea.
questions.concept: Hyponatraemia usually results from water excess relative to sodium.

followUp.q: A patient has plasma osmolality 252 mOsm/kg and a urine osmolality of 480 mOsm/kg with normal volume status. What does this suggest?
options: ADH is acting inappropriately (as in SIADH)
followUp.why: With low plasma osmolality ADH should be suppressed and urine dilute; a concentrated urine means ADH is acting. In primary polydipsia and diabetes insipidus the urine would be dilute.

questions.q: A 30-year-old with nephrotic syndrome has swollen ankles and periorbital oedema. Which change in Starling forces is the main cause?
options: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from albumin loss
questions.why: Heavy proteinuria lowers plasma albumin and so oncotic pressure, which normally retains fluid in capillaries. Net filtration rises and fluid accumulates in tissues. This is the classical explanation; primary renal sodium retention also contributes and may dominate in some patients, but of the options given only the fall in oncotic pressure is a correct Starling-force change.
optWhy: Correct: urinary albumin loss lowers capillary oncotic pressure so less fluid is reabsorbed.
Oncotic pressure falls in nephrotic syndrome; if it rose, fluid would be drawn into capillaries.
This would reduce filtration; it does not cause oedema.
Reduced permeability would reduce oedema; the problem is protein lost in urine.
questions.clue: Nephrotic syndrome with oedema.
questions.concept: Low plasma albumin lowers oncotic pressure and causes oedema.

followUp.q: Which change causes the oedema of right heart failure?
options: Increased venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure
followUp.why: A failing right heart raises systemic venous pressure, which raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and pushes fluid into the tissues. Albumin and oncotic pressure are not primarily altered.

questions.q: An 84-year-old resident of a care home with fever and poor intake is thirsty, confused and has dry mucous membranes. Sodium is 156 mmol/L. What is the main mechanism of the raised sodium?
options: Loss of water in excess of sodium, a net water deficit
Excess sodium intake with normal water balance
questions.why: Fever increases insensible loss and poor intake prevents replacement, so the ECF becomes hypertonic. Water leaves cells, causing thirst and confusion.
optWhy: Possible but uncommon; here poor intake, fever and dry membranes point to water loss.
Excess ADH causes hyponatraemia, not hypernatraemia.
Correct: hypernatraemia reflects a water deficit relative to sodium.
Overhydration with water lowers sodium; there is no such history.
questions.clue: Fever, poor intake, dry mucous membranes, sodium 156.
questions.concept: Hypernatraemia is a relative water deficit.

followUp.q: Why does acute hypernatraemia cause neurological symptoms?
options: Water enters brain cells, swelling them
Water leaves brain cells down the osmotic gradient, shrinking them
Potassium is lost from the extracellular fluid
followUp.why: A hypertonic ECF draws water out of cells, and shrinkage of brain cells causes confusion. Swelling is the problem in hyponatraemia, and the other mechanisms are not the main cause.

questions.q: Explain how a rise in plasma osmolality is detected and corrected.
markScheme: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise in plasma osmolality
They stimulate thirst, increasing water intake
They stimulate ADH release from the posterior pituitary
ADH inserts aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct so water is reabsorbed and urine is concentrated
Water retained dilutes plasma, restoring osmolality; negative feedback switches the response off
questions.modelAnswer: A rise in plasma osmolality is detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus. They trigger two responses. First, thirst, which increases water intake. Second, release of ADH (vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary. ADH acts on collecting duct cells, inserting aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane, so water is reabsorbed down the osmotic gradient of the renal medulla and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced. The retained and ingested water dilutes the plasma, restoring its osmolality towards normal, and the fall in osmolality switches off the stimuli by negative feedback.
questions.concept: Osmoreceptor, ADH and thirst control of water balance.

questions.q: Which hormone is released by atrial stretch and promotes urinary sodium excretion?
questions.why: ANP is the counterpart to the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and reduces volume when the atria are stretched.
optWhy: It increases sodium reabsorption.
It increases water reabsorption and has little direct effect on sodium excretion.
It is an enzyme from juxtaglomerular cells that starts the system conserving sodium.
Correct: ANP is released in response to atrial stretch and promotes sodium excretion.
questions.clue: Released by atrial stretch, promotes sodium excretion.
questions.concept: ANP promotes natriuresis.

followUp.q: Which hormone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct to increase sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion?
followUp.why: Aldosterone acts on principal cells to increase sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. ANP does the opposite for sodium, ADH acts on water channels, and parathyroid hormone regulates calcium.

questions.q: A 67-year-old has chronic kidney disease and takes an ACE inhibitor and a potassium-sparing diuretic. Potassium is 6.8 mmol/L and the ECG shows peaked T waves. What is the effect of raised extracellular potassium on cardiac cells?
options: It partially depolarises the resting membrane potential, impairing repolarisation and conduction
It hyperpolarises cells, making them harder to excite
It has no effect on the resting membrane potential
It increases the gradient for potassium leaving the cell and so strengthens contraction
questions.why: Raised extracellular potassium reduces the potassium gradient, making the resting potential less negative. Cells partly depolarise, sodium channels inactivate and repolarisation is impaired, so conduction slows and arrhythmias can occur; peaked T waves are an early ECG sign.
optWhy: Correct: a less negative resting potential inactivates sodium channels and disrupts conduction.
Hyperpolarisation occurs with low extracellular potassium.
Potassium gradients are the main determinant of resting membrane potential.
Raising extracellular potassium reduces the gradient for potassium leaving the cell.
questions.clue: Potassium 6.8 mmol/L with peaked T waves.
questions.concept: Hyperkalaemia depolarises excitable cells.

followUp.q: What effect does low extracellular potassium have on the resting membrane potential?
options: It abolishes the resting membrane potential
followUp.why: A larger gradient for potassium to leave makes the resting potential more negative, so cells are less excitable and muscle weakness and arrhythmias occur.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man is brought in after a road traffic accident with a heart rate of 130 beats/min and a falling blood pressure; he has lost roughly 1.5 L of blood. Which combination of hormonal responses is expected?
options: Decreased renin and aldosterone to promote sodium loss
Increased ANP to promote sodium excretion
Decreased ADH to promote water excretion
Increased renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone and ADH, retaining sodium and water
questions.why: Reduced renal perfusion and sympathetic activation release renin; angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and aldosterone release, and baroreceptor unloading stimulates ADH. The aim is to restore volume and pressure.
optWhy: Volume depletion increases renin and aldosterone to conserve sodium.
ANP is released by atrial stretch and would fall with volume depletion.
A large volume loss stimulates ADH release to conserve water.
Correct: falling renal perfusion and baroreceptor unloading activate the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and ADH.
questions.clue: Heart rate 130, falling blood pressure, loss of 1.5 L of blood.
questions.concept: Haemorrhage activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and ADH.

followUp.q: Atrial stretch in a patient with fluid overload would be expected to cause which hormonal change?
followUp.why: Stretch of the atria releases ANP, promoting sodium and water loss. Renin and aldosterone would be suppressed in volume overload, and ANP would not fall.

questions.q: A 78-year-old is nil by mouth after surgery, with no signs of hypovolaemia and a normal U&E. Which statement fits the NICE principles for IV fluids?
options: Use tetrastarch as the preferred fluid for any hypovolaemia
Give as much fluid as possible to prevent acute kidney injury
Add potassium directly to the bag on the ward as a routine
If IV fluids are needed for routine maintenance, start with a restricted prescription of water, electrolytes and glucose and review at least daily
questions.why: CG174 stresses assessing needs at every review, using IV fluids only if oral or enteral routes cannot meet them, starting maintenance as a restricted prescription of water, electrolytes and glucose, and reviewing at least daily. No volumes are given here.
optWhy: Excess fluid causes harm; CG174 favours a restricted maintenance prescription.
Potassium is not added directly to bags on the ward; premixed bags are used.
Correct: this reflects CG174's approach to routine maintenance.
CG174 says tetrastarch is not used for fluid resuscitation.
questions.clue: Nil by mouth post-operatively, no hypovolaemia, normal U&E.
questions.concept: NICE principles for routine maintenance fluids.

followUp.q: Which type of fluid does CG174 recommend for fluid resuscitation?
followUp.why: Resuscitation uses sodium-containing crystalloids in that range. Tetrastarch is not used, 5% glucose alone is hypotonic and not suitable for resuscitation, and albumin is considered only in severe sepsis.

questions.q: Describe how the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system restores extracellular fluid volume after a fall in blood pressure, and the role of atrial natriuretic peptide.
markScheme: Fall in renal perfusion, reduced NaCl delivery or sympathetic stimulation releases renin from juxtaglomerular cells
Renin leads to angiotensin II, which causes vasoconstriction and stimulates thirst and aldosterone release
Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the distal tubule and collecting duct, with water following, and potassium secretion
Retained sodium and water restore ECF volume and blood pressure
ANP is released by atrial stretch when volume is high and promotes sodium excretion, opposing the system
questions.modelAnswer: A fall in blood pressure or renal perfusion, reduced sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa, or sympathetic stimulation causes juxtaglomerular cells to release renin. Renin acts on angiotensinogen, and angiotensin-converting enzyme then produces angiotensin II. Angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor that raises blood pressure quickly; it also stimulates thirst and the release of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex. Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct to increase sodium reabsorption, with water following osmotically, and to increase potassium secretion. The retained sodium and water restore ECF volume and blood pressure. Atrial natriuretic peptide, released when atrial stretch signals a high volume, promotes sodium excretion and vasodilatation, so it opposes the system and prevents excessive volume expansion.
questions.concept: Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and ANP.

questions.q: Which structure senses the delivery of sodium chloride to the distal tubule and signals to adjust the afferent arteriole and renin release?
options: The principal cells of the collecting duct
questions.why: The macula densa lies in the wall of the distal tubule next to the glomerulus. It detects sodium chloride delivery and signals the afferent arteriole and the juxtaglomerular cells.
optWhy: They release renin, but they are the effector, not the sensor of tubular sodium chloride.
Correct: its cells sense sodium chloride delivery and drive tubuloglomerular feedback.
They form the filtration slits and do not sense tubular fluid composition.
They respond to aldosterone and ADH; they do not control the afferent arteriole.
questions.clue: Sensor of distal sodium chloride delivery.
questions.concept: Tubuloglomerular feedback senses sodium chloride delivery.

followUp.q: Which cells release renin?
options: Juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole
Intercalated cells of the collecting duct
followUp.why: Juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole secrete renin when perfusion, sympathetic activity or sodium chloride delivery changes. The macula densa senses delivery, podocytes form the filtration barrier, and intercalated cells secrete acid.

questions.q: A urine sample has creatinine 6 mmol/L, the urine flow rate is 2 mL/min and plasma creatinine is 0.1 mmol/L. What is the creatinine clearance?
questions.why: Clearance = U × V ÷ P. With U = 6 mmol/L, V = 2 mL/min and P = 0.1 mmol/L, C = 12 ÷ 0.1 = 120 mL/min, close to a normal GFR.
optWhy: Correct: 6 × 2 ÷ 0.1 = 120 mL/min.
This is the product of urine concentration and flow (6 × 2) without dividing by the plasma concentration.
This multiplies by the plasma concentration instead of dividing by it.
This is the ratio of urine to plasma concentration (6 ÷ 0.1) without multiplying by the urine flow rate.
questions.clue: Clearance = UV/P.
questions.concept: Clearance calculation.

followUp.q: If a substance is freely filtered and also secreted by the tubule, how does its clearance compare with GFR?
options: It cannot be compared with GFR
followUp.why: Secretion adds to what is filtered, so more is excreted than the filtered amount and clearance exceeds GFR. Reabsorption would make clearance lower, and only a substance that is neither reabsorbed nor secreted has clearance equal to GFR.

questions.q: A man's serum creatinine was 82 µmol/L on admission and is 111 µmol/L 36 hours later. Urine output has not been measured. Using NICE NG148, how should this be interpreted?
options: It meets the AKI criteria, because the rise is 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours
It does not meet the criteria, because the creatinine must double
It does not meet the criteria, because the rise is less than 50%
It cannot be classified without a urine output measurement
questions.why: The rise is 111 − 82 = 29 µmol/L within 48 hours, which meets the criterion of 26 µmol/L or more. The ratio is 111 ÷ 82 = 1.35, below 1.5, but the criteria are alternatives. The staging algorithm would then place this as stage 1.
optWhy: The 50% criterion is one of three alternatives; an absolute rise of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours is enough on its own.
Any one of the three criteria is sufficient; urine output is not needed.
Correct: the absolute rise is 29 µmol/L within 48 hours.
A doubling is the threshold for stage 2 severity, not for detecting AKI.
questions.clue: Creatinine 82 to 111 in 36 hours.
questions.concept: AKI criteria are alternatives.

followUp.q: A 70 kg patient passes 20 mL of urine per hour for 8 hours. Does this meet the NG148 urine output criterion?
options: No: the criterion is below 0.5 mL per hour, which is not met
Yes: 20 ÷ 70 = 0.29 mL/kg/hour, below 0.5 for more than 6 hours
No: only a total below 400 mL in 24 hours counts as oliguria
No: the output must stay below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours
followUp.why: The criterion is per kilogram: 0.5 × 70 = 35 mL/h is the threshold, and 20 mL/h for 8 hours is below it for more than 6 hours. Below 400 mL in 24 hours is a traditional definition of oliguria, not the NG148 criterion, and 12 hours is not the NG148 time frame.

questions.q: A 68-year-old taking ramipril and ibuprofen has vomiting and diarrhoea and is volume depleted. Creatinine has risen from 84 to 190 µmol/L. Which explanation of the fall in GFR is correct?
options: Ibuprofen dilates the afferent arteriole, which reduces filtration
Fluid loss raises capsular hydrostatic pressure, opposing filtration
Reduced perfusion, with ibuprofen removing afferent dilation and ramipril removing efferent constriction, so glomerular pressure falls
Ramipril constricts the efferent arteriole, lowering the pressure upstream
questions.why: When perfusion is low, the kidney protects GFR through prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation and angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction. NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors block these, so glomerular hydrostatic pressure and GFR fall. At 2.26 times baseline this is stage 2.
optWhy: Correct: both arterioles' compensatory adjustments are blocked at a time when they are needed.
ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II and so dilate the efferent arteriole; efferent constriction would raise glomerular pressure.
Ibuprofen inhibits prostaglandin synthesis and so removes afferent dilation; afferent dilation would raise filtration.
Capsular pressure rises with urinary obstruction, not with volume loss.
questions.clue: ACE inhibitor, NSAID, volume depletion.
questions.concept: Drugs that disturb autoregulation.

followUp.q: Which pairing of arteriole and mediator correctly describes autoregulation under low perfusion?
options: Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole
Prostaglandins constrict the afferent arteriole and angiotensin II dilates the efferent arteriole
Angiotensin II dilates the afferent arteriole and prostaglandins constrict the efferent arteriole
Both prostaglandins and angiotensin II constrict the afferent arteriole
followUp.why: Afferent dilation increases inflow, and efferent constriction raises the pressure behind the glomerulus; both maintain filtration when perfusion is low.

questions.q: A patient has had an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73 m² and a urine ACR of 45 mg/mmol on repeated tests over 5 months. Using NICE NG203 categories, what is the classification?
questions.why: CKD requires abnormality for more than 3 months, here 5 months. G3b is 30–44 and A3 is above 30 mg/mmol, so the person has G3b A3 CKD.
optWhy: G3a is 45–59 and A2 is 3–30 mg/mmol; both categories are too mild.
G4 is 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m²; 38 is above that range.
The GFR category is right, but A2 is 3–30 mg/mmol and an ACR of 45 is above it.
Correct: GFR 30–44 is G3b and ACR above 30 mg/mmol is A3; the abnormality has lasted more than 3 months.
questions.clue: eGFR 38, ACR 45, 5 months.
questions.concept: NG203 classification.

followUp.q: Which finding is required before kidney abnormalities are called chronic kidney disease?
options: They have been present for more than 7 days
They are accompanied by a creatinine above 200 µmol/L
They have been present for more than 3 months
followUp.why: Chronicity (more than 3 months) separates CKD from AKI. Oliguria and a specific creatinine are not required, and 7 days is the AKI window for the 50% criterion.

questions.q: Explain how the kidney keeps GFR stable when arterial pressure changes, and how NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors can disturb this.
markScheme: Myogenic response: the afferent arteriole constricts when stretched by a rising pressure and relaxes when pressure falls
Tubuloglomerular feedback: the macula densa senses sodium chloride delivery and adjusts afferent tone and renin release
When perfusion falls, prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole to preserve glomerular pressure
NSAIDs remove afferent dilation
ACE inhibitors remove efferent constriction, so GFR can fall sharply, especially with volume depletion
questions.modelAnswer: Autoregulation keeps GFR approximately constant across a wide range of mean arterial pressure. In the myogenic response, the afferent arteriole contracts when it is stretched by a higher pressure and relaxes when pressure falls. In tubuloglomerular feedback, the macula densa senses the delivery of sodium chloride to the distal tubule; high delivery constricts the afferent arteriole, while low delivery releases renin and dilates the afferent arteriole. When perfusion falls, prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, preserving glomerular hydrostatic pressure. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis and so remove afferent dilation, and ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II and so remove efferent constriction. In a volume-depleted patient taking both, glomerular pressure and GFR can fall sharply, causing acute kidney injury.
questions.concept: Autoregulation of GFR and drug effects.

questions.q: Which is the main buffer system of the extracellular fluid?
questions.why: The bicarbonate system is the main extracellular buffer because both of its components can be adjusted: CO₂ by ventilation and bicarbonate by the kidney.
optWhy: It is important in urine and inside cells, but extracellular phosphate is low.
It carries acid in the urine and is not the main blood buffer.
It buffers hydrogen ions released in the red cell, but it does not account for the main extracellular buffering.
Correct: it is the main extracellular buffer, regulated by the kidneys and lungs.
questions.clue: Main extracellular buffer.
questions.concept: Bicarbonate is the main ECF buffer.

followUp.q: After buffering, which response to an acid load acts next, within minutes?
options: A change in ventilation that alters PaCO₂
followUp.why: Chemoreceptors adjust ventilation within minutes. Renal changes take hours to days, and urea synthesis or bone release of calcium are not rapid regulators of pH.

questions.q: A patient has bicarbonate 12 mmol/L and PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa, with no respiratory compensation. Using pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻] ÷ (0.225 × PaCO₂)), what is the pH?
questions.why: With bicarbonate 12 and no change in PaCO₂, the ratio falls to about 10:1, so the pH falls by 0.3 units. The calculation gives 6.1 + 1.00 = 7.10. A pH of 7.10 shows why metabolic acidosis triggers hyperventilation.
optWhy: This assumes the pH is normal; with bicarbonate halved and PaCO₂ unchanged the ratio falls from 20:1 to 10:1.
This leaves out the 0.225 solubility factor (log₁₀ of 12 ÷ 5.3 = 0.35, giving 6.45).
This uses the natural logarithm instead of base 10.
questions.clue: Bicarbonate 12, PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa.
questions.concept: Henderson–Hasselbalch calculation.

followUp.q: What is the expected respiratory response to this metabolic acidosis?
followUp.why: Acidaemia stimulates chemoreceptors and increases ventilation, blowing off CO₂ and raising the ratio. Hypoventilation would worsen the acidosis, and renal retention of bicarbonate is the response to respiratory acidosis.

questions.q: A 19-year-old with diabetic ketoacidosis has pH 7.12, PaCO₂ 2.4 kPa, bicarbonate 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L and chloride 98 mmol/L. Winter's formula predicts a PaCO₂ of 1.9–2.5 kPa. Which interpretation fits?
options: A normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
A raised anion gap metabolic acidosis (gap 30.4) with appropriate respiratory compensation
A respiratory alkalosis, because PaCO₂ is low
A mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis
questions.why: The pH of 7.12 is acidaemic and the low bicarbonate explains it, so the primary disorder is metabolic. The gap of 134 − 98 − 5.6 = 30.4 is raised by ketoanions. The PaCO₂ of 2.4 kPa (18 mmHg) lies within 1.9–2.5 kPa, so the lungs are compensating as expected.
optWhy: Correct: bicarbonate is low, the gap is raised and the measured PaCO₂ lies in the predicted range.
The pH is acidaemic, so the low PaCO₂ is the compensation, not the primary process.
PaCO₂ is low, not high; a coexisting respiratory acidosis would give a PaCO₂ above the predicted range.
134 − 98 − 5.6 = 30.4 mmol/L is well above the typical range of roughly 8–16.
questions.clue: DKA gas with low PaCO₂.
questions.concept: Interpreting an arterial blood gas.

followUp.q: A patient with a similar gas has a PaCO₂ of 4.0 kPa. What does this suggest?
options: Inadequate respiratory compensation, which may reflect exhaustion or a coexisting respiratory problem
followUp.why: 4.0 kPa is above the predicted 1.9–2.5, so the patient is not breathing enough to compensate; the clinical team would watch closely. A value below the range would suggest a coexisting respiratory alkalosis.

questions.q: A man has had repeated vomiting for three days. Gas: pH 7.52, PaCO₂ 6.4 kPa, bicarbonate 38 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L. Which statement is correct?
options: It is a metabolic alkalosis, and the raised PaCO₂ is compensatory hypoventilation
It is a respiratory acidosis, because PaCO₂ is high
It is caused by bicarbonate loss in the vomit
It is a respiratory failure from chronic lung disease
questions.why: The pH is above 7.45 and the bicarbonate is raised, so the primary process is metabolic alkalosis. Reduced ventilation raises PaCO₂ to limit the alkalosis. Gastric acid loss, volume contraction and potassium loss all maintain it.
