optWhy: Correct: high bicarbonate with alkalaemia is metabolic, and the raised PaCO₂ is the expected, limited compensation.
The pH is alkalaemic, so a respiratory acidosis would be expected to lower pH.
Vomit contains gastric acid; the loss of H⁺ leaves excess bicarbonate.
Nothing in the data suggests lung disease; PaCO₂ rises to compensate for alkalosis.
questions.clue: pH 7.52, bicarbonate 38, potassium 2.9.
questions.concept: Metabolic alkalosis and compensation.

followUp.q: Why does a metabolic alkalosis with volume contraction cause low potassium?
options: Potassium is lost directly in gastric acid
Aldosterone-driven renal potassium loss and potassium moving into cells in alkalosis
Alkalosis blocks potassium absorption in the gut
Insulin falls and potassium moves out of cells
followUp.why: Volume contraction raises aldosterone, which promotes potassium secretion, and alkalosis shifts potassium into cells. Gastric juice contains only a little potassium, and the other options are not the main mechanisms.

questions.q: A patient with COPD has pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 8.6 kPa, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L and PaO₂ 7.9 kPa. What does the raised bicarbonate show?
options: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis
Renal compensation for chronic CO₂ retention in a respiratory acidosis
questions.why: A high PaCO₂ with acidaemia is a respiratory acidosis. A raised bicarbonate with only a mild fall in pH indicates the kidney has had days to retain bicarbonate, so the disorder is chronic, though this may be acute-on-chronic if a recent deterioration is suspected.
optWhy: Correct: the kidney retains bicarbonate over days to limit the fall in pH.
The pH is acidaemic, so the primary process is not alkalosis.
In an acute disorder, bicarbonate would be near normal because the kidney has not had time to respond.
A metabolic acidosis would show a low bicarbonate and a low PaCO₂.
questions.clue: COPD, high PaCO₂, raised bicarbonate.
questions.concept: Renal compensation for respiratory acidosis.

followUp.q: Over what time scale does renal compensation develop?
followUp.why: The renal response builds over hours and reaches its maximum over several days. Buffering is immediate and ventilation changes in minutes, and months are not needed.

questions.q: A patient has a metabolic acidosis. Explain how the body compensates and why the compensation is incomplete.
markScheme: Acidaemia stimulates chemoreceptors and increases ventilation (Kussmaul breathing)
Hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂, raising the bicarbonate to CO₂ ratio and pH
The kidney excretes more acid, as ammonium and titratable acid, and generates new bicarbonate, over hours to days
Compensation is incomplete because the stimulus for ventilation is lost once pH returns toward normal and ventilation is limited by work of breathing and oxygenation
A persistent cause, for example ketoacidosis, continues to add acid
questions.modelAnswer: In metabolic acidosis the low pH stimulates peripheral and central chemoreceptors, increasing ventilation (Kussmaul breathing in diabetic ketoacidosis). Hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂, which raises the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved CO₂ in the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation and so pH. Winter's formula predicts the expected PaCO₂. Over hours to days the kidney also excretes more acid, buffered as ammonium and phosphate, and generates new bicarbonate. Compensation is incomplete because the respiratory drive falls as pH approaches normal, ventilation is limited by the work of breathing, and the underlying process, such as ketone production, continues to add acid until the cause is treated.
questions.concept: Respiratory and renal compensation in metabolic acidosis.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man taking an ACE inhibitor and ibuprofen is admitted after two days of vomiting and diarrhoea with a creatinine of 190 µmol/L (baseline 84). Explain the pathophysiology of his acute kidney injury, how it is recognised and staged, and the principles of its management.
markScheme: Volume loss reduces renal perfusion and glomerular filtration (pre-renal state); tubules intact, urine concentrated, urea:creatinine above about 100
Autoregulation normally preserves GFR: prostaglandin afferent dilation and angiotensin II efferent constriction; tubuloglomerular feedback
NSAID removes afferent dilation and ACE inhibitor removes efferent constriction, so glomerular hydrostatic pressure and GFR fall
Prolonged hypoperfusion may progress to acute tubular necrosis, where concentrating ability is lost
NG148 criteria: creatinine rise of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours, 50% or more within 7 days, urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours
UKKA staging by ratio to baseline: 190 ÷ 84 = 2.26, stage 2

Management principles: assess volume status and cause, restore volume with IV fluid and reassess, review or withhold nephrotoxic and haemodynamically active drugs, exclude obstruction, check urine dipstick, monitor urine output, potassium and acid–base
Complications to monitor: hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload; follow-up of renal function after recovery
questions.modelAnswer: Vomiting and diarrhoea reduce extracellular volume and so renal perfusion. The kidney normally protects GFR through autoregulation: prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, and tubuloglomerular feedback adjusts afferent tone. Ibuprofen removes afferent dilation and the ACE inhibitor removes efferent constriction, so glomerular hydrostatic pressure and GFR fall, producing a pre-renal AKI with intact tubules, concentrated urine and a high urea:creatinine ratio; prolonged hypoperfusion can progress to acute tubular necrosis. NICE NG148 recognises AKI by a rise in creatinine of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours, a rise of 50% or more within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours. Staged by ratio to baseline (UK Kidney Association), 190 ÷ 84 = 2.26 is stage 2. Management addresses the cause: assess volume status, restore volume with IV fluid and frequent reassessment, withhold the nephrotoxic and haemodynamically active drugs, exclude obstruction, dipstick the urine (blood, protein, leucocytes, nitrites and glucose), and monitor urine output, potassium and acid–base balance for complications such as hyperkalaemia and acidosis. Renal function is rechecked after recovery. No volumes or rates are given here because they follow the patient and local protocol.
questions.concept: Pre-renal AKI, autoregulation and NG148 criteria.

questions.q: Describe how insulin and glucagon regulate blood glucose in the fed and fasting states, and explain how absolute insulin deficiency leads to diabetic ketoacidosis and its clinical features.
markScheme: Fed state: rising glucose stimulates beta-cell insulin release, promoting glucose uptake (GLUT4 in muscle and fat), glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis and protein synthesis, and suppressing glucose output
Fasting: falling insulin and rising glucagon increase glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and, with prolonged fasting, ketogenesis
Absolute insulin deficiency: glucose cannot enter muscle and fat, the liver makes more glucose, and glucagon effects go unopposed
Hyperglycaemia exceeds the renal threshold, causing osmotic diuresis, polyuria, thirst, dehydration and electrolyte loss
Unopposed lipolysis supplies fatty acids that the liver converts to ketone bodies, which are acids, causing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis
Compensation: Kussmaul breathing lowers PaCO₂; vomiting and abdominal pain; potassium shifts out of cells so plasma potassium may be normal or high despite total body depletion
JBDS principles: fluids, insulin infusion, potassium monitoring and replacement, treat the precipitant; no doses stated
Structure with correct use of values labelled approximate
questions.modelAnswer: After a meal, rising glucose stimulates insulin release from pancreatic beta cells. Insulin promotes glucose uptake into muscle and fat through GLUT4, glycogen synthesis in liver and muscle, lipogenesis and protein synthesis, and suppresses hepatic glucose output, lipolysis and ketogenesis. In the fasting state insulin falls and glucagon rises, which stimulates glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and lipolysis, and in prolonged fasting ketogenesis. In absolute insulin deficiency, as in type 1 diabetes, glucose cannot enter muscle and fat and the liver overproduces glucose, so glucose rises. Once it exceeds the renal threshold, osmotic diuresis causes polyuria, thirst, dehydration and loss of sodium and potassium. Unopposed lipolysis supplies fatty acids that the liver converts to ketone bodies, acids that consume bicarbonate and cause a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. The low pH stimulates deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing to lower PaCO₂, and vomiting and abdominal pain are common. Lack of insulin and acidosis move potassium out of cells, so plasma potassium may be normal or raised although total body potassium is low, and it falls when insulin is given. Treatment follows JBDS-based protocols: restore volume, give a continuous insulin infusion to stop ketogenesis, monitor and replace potassium, and look for the precipitating cause. No doses are given here.
questions.concept: Insulin and glucagon actions and the mechanism of diabetic ketoacidosis.

cases.title: Vomiting, diarrhoea and a rising creatinine

steps.text: A 68-year-old man presents after two days of vomiting and diarrhoea. He feels dizzy on standing and has passed very little urine today. He takes ramipril for hypertension, ibuprofen for knee pain and a statin. He has no history of kidney disease; a blood test six months ago showed creatinine 84 µmol/L.

ask.q: Which part of his drug history matters most for his kidneys at this point?
options: The statin, because statins are the usual cause of acute kidney injury
Ramipril and ibuprofen, because both interfere with the kidney's protection of GFR when perfusion is low
None of them, because drugs only matter in chronic kidney disease
Only the ibuprofen, because ACE inhibitors never affect the kidney
ask.why: An ACE inhibitor removes efferent constriction and an NSAID removes afferent dilation, so together with volume depletion they can drop glomerular pressure. Statins are not a usual cause of AKI, drugs matter in AKI as well as CKD, and ACE inhibitors do affect autoregulation.

steps.text: On examination he is dry, with heart rate 108 beats/min, supine blood pressure 96/58 mmHg and a postural drop, cool peripheries and no oedema; the bladder is not palpable. Urine dipstick shows trace protein and no blood. Blood results: sodium 146, potassium 5.4, urea 21.3 mmol/L, creatinine 190 µmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L.

ask.q: Using the baseline of 84 µmol/L, what stage of AKI is this by the UK Kidney Association algorithm?
options: Stage 1: it is more than 26 µmol/L above baseline
It cannot be staged without a urine output measurement
ask.why: Stage is set by the ratio to baseline: 1.5–1.9 times is stage 1, 2.0–2.9 times is stage 2 and 3.0 times or more is stage 3. A rise of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours counts as stage 1 only when the ratio is below 1.5, and here the baseline is six months old and the ratio is 2.26, and the creatinine criterion can be used without urine output. The urea:creatinine ratio is about 112, a pre-renal pattern.

steps.text: The picture is of volume depletion with pre-renal acute kidney injury, worsened by ramipril and ibuprofen. There is no sign of obstruction, and the urine dipstick shows no blood.

ask.q: Which set of actions best reflects the principles of managing this patient?
options: Give a diuretic to start urine flow, since low urine output means fluid overload
Continue all medicines and wait for oral intake to recover
Assess volume status, replace the deficit with IV fluid under frequent reassessment, withhold ramipril and ibuprofen for now, and monitor urine output and potassium
Arrange dialysis immediately because the creatinine has doubled
ask.why: Treating the cause means restoring perfusion while reviewing nephrotoxic and haemodynamically active drugs, with close monitoring (NICE NG148). A diuretic would deepen volume depletion, continuing the drugs would prolong the insult, and a doubled creatinine alone is not an indication for dialysis. Volumes and rates depend on the patient and local protocol, so none are given here.

steps.text: After 48 hours of treatment, the creatinine has fallen to 112 µmol/L, potassium is 4.6 mmol/L and he is passing urine normally. The ramipril is restarted later with a repeat U&E planned, and he is advised to avoid NSAIDs.

debrief: AKI is recognised from the creatinine (a rise of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours, or 50% or more within 7 days) or from low urine output, and staged by the ratio to baseline.
Pre-renal injury follows reduced perfusion; ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs and diuretics make the kidney vulnerable by removing autoregulatory protection.
Management principles: find and treat the cause, restore volume with reassessment, review nephrotoxic drugs, check for obstruction and monitor potassium and urine output.
No fluid volumes, rates or doses are given here; they follow the individual patient and local protocol.

cases.title: Thirst, weight loss and deep breathing

steps.text: A 19-year-old student has had three weeks of thirst, passing a lot of urine and losing weight, and today has vomiting and abdominal pain. He breathes deeply and rapidly without wheeze or chest signs. He has no known diabetes.

ask.q: What best explains the deep, sighing breathing?
options: Panic-related hyperventilation causing a respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis (Kussmaul breathing)
ask.why: A rise in acid load lowers pH, stimulates chemoreceptors and increases ventilation to lower PaCO₂. The picture of weight loss, polyuria and vomiting points to ketoacidosis, and there are no chest signs to suggest pneumonia or pulmonary oedema.

steps.text: Bedside tests: capillary glucose 28 mmol/L and blood ketones 5.8 mmol/L. A venous gas shows pH 7.08 and bicarbonate 6 mmol/L; potassium is 5.6 mmol/L.

ask.q: Which result most clearly separates diabetic ketoacidosis from simple hyperglycaemia?
options: The raised blood ketones together with low pH and bicarbonate
The glucose of 28 mmol/L on its own
ask.why: Ketoacidosis needs ketone production plus acidosis, which the ketones, pH and bicarbonate show. A high glucose also occurs in hyperglycaemia without acidosis, potassium is influenced by many factors, and vomiting is a symptom, not a test result. The JBDS guideline uses raised ketones with a low bicarbonate or pH, together with high glucose or known diabetes.

steps.text: His potassium is 5.6 mmol/L, yet the team treats him as potassium-depleted.

ask.q: Why is plasma potassium raised although total body potassium is low?
options: Excess dietary potassium has built up over three weeks
Ketones directly make the kidney retain potassium
Lack of insulin and acidosis move potassium out of cells, while osmotic diuresis and vomiting remove potassium from the body
Total body potassium is high, so potassium is never given
ask.why: Without insulin, potassium cannot enter cells and acidosis shifts it out, so plasma potassium looks normal or high while body stores are depleted by urinary losses. Plasma potassium will fall once insulin is given and acidosis corrects, so it is monitored closely and replaced as needed.

steps.text: The team follows a local protocol based on the Joint British Diabetes Societies guideline.

ask.q: Which statement describes the principles of treatment?
options: Give bicarbonate first to correct the pH, and use insulin later
Restore circulating volume with IV fluid, give a continuous insulin infusion to switch off ketone production, monitor and replace potassium, and look for the precipitating cause
Give subcutaneous insulin and send him home once glucose falls
Stop the insulin infusion as soon as the glucose is below 14 mmol/L, because DKA is then resolved
ask.why: Insulin is needed to stop ketogenesis, and glucose is added while insulin continues until ketones and acidosis clear, because glucose can fall before ketones do. Bicarbonate is not routine, and discharge needs resolved ketoacidosis and diabetes education. No doses or rates are given here.

steps.text: Over the next day the ketones fall and the pH returns towards normal. He starts regular insulin, is taught about diabetes and is seen by the diabetes team before discharge. A precipitating cause, here a new presentation of type 1 diabetes, is recorded.

debrief: DKA is a triad: hyperglycaemia (or known diabetes), ketonaemia and acidosis.
Kussmaul breathing is respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis, not a lung problem.
Plasma potassium may be normal or high at presentation despite total body depletion, and it falls with insulin.
Insulin continues until ketones clear; glucose normalising does not mean DKA has resolved.
No doses are given here; follow current JBDS-based local protocols.

interpret.title: U&E in an older woman with pneumonia
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 79-year-old woman with pneumonia has barely drunk for three days and is thirsty and confused. Her creatinine six months ago was 80 µmol/L. Which interpretation fits best? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: SIADH, with water retention diluting sodium
A water deficit with hypernatraemia and a pre-renal pattern: raised osmolality (316) and urea:creatinine above 100
A hyperosmolar state driven by glucose
Fluid overload from excess intravenous fluid
interpret.why: Calculated osmolality = 2 × 148 + 5.2 + 14.8 = 316 mOsm/kg, above the typical 285–295 range. Urea:creatinine = 14.8 × 1000 ÷ 128 = 115.6, above about 100, favouring reduced perfusion with urea reabsorbed along with water. The creatinine of 128 against a baseline of 80 (1.6 times) would also need checking against the AKI criteria.
optWhy: SIADH lowers sodium; here sodium is raised.
Correct: sodium, urea and calculated osmolality are raised, and the ratio of 115.6 points to a pre-renal state.
Glucose is 5.2 mmol/L; the raised osmolality comes from sodium and urea.
Overload would dilute sodium; the thirst, confusion and raised urea point to a deficit.

interpret.title: Low sodium in a clinically euvolaemic patient
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 71-year-old with a small-cell lung lesion is euvolaemic, takes no diuretics and has a normal thyroid and adrenal function. Which interpretation is best? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: True hypotonic hyponatraemia with an inappropriately concentrated urine and urinary sodium loss, consistent with SIADH
Hyperglycaemia drawing water out of cells
interpret.why: Calculated osmolality = 2 × 122 + 5.0 + 3.1 = 252.1 mOsm/kg, which agrees with the measured 250 and confirms hypotonic hyponatraemia. When serum osmolality is low, ADH should be switched off and the urine dilute; a urine osmolality of 420 means water is being retained, and the urine sodium of 62 in a euvolaemic person with the other causes excluded fits SIADH.
optWhy: In primary polydipsia ADH is suppressed, so the urine would be maximally dilute, not 420.
Correct: low serum osmolality with a urine osmolality of 420 shows ADH is acting, and the urinary sodium is high in a euvolaemic patient.
Measured osmolality would be normal; here it is low, at 250.
Glucose is 5.0 mmol/L, so it cannot explain a fall in sodium.

interpret.title: Screening in an asymptomatic adult
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 52-year-old man with no symptoms has these results. The HbA1c bands usually quoted are below 42 (lower risk), 42–47 (high risk of diabetes) and 48 or above (diabetes range); a fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 or above is in the diabetes range. What is the best interpretation? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: Pre-diabetes, because the values are close to normal
Inconclusive, because HbA1c is unreliable with a normal haemoglobin
The criteria for diabetes are met, with two results in the diabetes range and a normal haemoglobin
Normal, because the person has no symptoms
interpret.why: 52 and 54 mmol/mol are both at or above 48, and the fasting glucose of 7.6 exceeds 7.0. Without symptoms, a repeat abnormal result confirms diabetes, which here has been obtained. The classification into type 2 or other types rests on the clinical picture. These thresholds are guidance (WHO and Diabetes UK criteria, with NICE PH38 bands for high risk).
optWhy: Pre-diabetes would need an HbA1c of 42–47; both values are 48 or above.
Haemoglobin disorders and anaemias can distort HbA1c; a normal haemoglobin does not.
Correct: HbA1c 52 and 54 are at or above 48, and fasting glucose 7.6 is at or above 7.0.
Many people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms, and the results decide.

interpret.title: Blood gas in a septic patient
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 60-year-old with pneumonia and sepsis is tiring. Winter's formula predicts a PaCO₂ of 21–25 mmHg, which is 2.8–3.3 kPa. What is the best interpretation? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: A raised anion gap metabolic acidosis, with a PaCO₂ above the predicted range, suggesting inadequate respiratory compensation
A raised anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
interpret.why: Henderson–Hasselbalch check: 0.225 × 3.6 = 0.81; 10 ÷ 0.81 = 12.3; log₁₀ = 1.09; pH = 7.19. The bicarbonate of 10 gives expected PaCO₂ of 1.5 × 10 + 8 = 23 ± 2 mmHg, or 2.8–3.3 kPa. A PaCO₂ of 3.6 kPa (27 mmHg) is above this, so the patient is not ventilating enough to compensate; fatigue or lung disease may be contributing.
optWhy: Correct: the gap is 27, and 3.6 kPa is above the predicted 2.8–3.3.
Compensation would give a PaCO₂ of 2.8–3.3 kPa; 3.6 kPa is higher.
The pH is acidaemic, so the low PaCO₂ cannot be the primary disorder.
138 − 101 − 10 = 27 mmol/L, which is raised.

interpret.title: Blood gas after severe diarrhoea
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 45-year-old has had profuse watery diarrhoea for four days. Winter's formula predicts a PaCO₂ of 27–31 mmHg, which is 3.6–4.1 kPa. Which interpretation fits? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: A normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss in stool, with appropriate respiratory compensation
interpret.why: The anion gap is 138 − 114 − 14 = 10 mmol/L (normal). The pH is 6.1 + log₁₀(14 ÷ (0.225 × 3.9)) = 7.30. Stool is rich in bicarbonate, so diarrhoea loses bicarbonate and chloride rises to maintain electroneutrality. Expected PaCO₂ is 1.5 × 14 + 8 = 29 ± 2 mmHg (3.6–4.1 kPa), so compensation is appropriate.
optWhy: Correct: the gap is 10, chloride is raised, and the PaCO₂ of 3.9 is within the predicted range.
Ketoacidosis would raise the anion gap through ketoanions; here it is 10.
PaCO₂ is low, not high.
Lactic acidosis also raises the anion gap; the gap here is normal.

interpret.title: Liver blood tests in a jaundiced patient
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 74-year-old has itching, dark urine, pale stools and weight loss. Which interpretation and next step are most appropriate? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: A cholestatic pattern, with a raised GGT confirming a liver origin of the ALP; abdominal ultrasound to look for biliary obstruction
A hepatocellular pattern, so the first step is viral serology alone
Bone disease, because ALP is raised, so no liver investigation is needed
Mild abnormalities to be repeated in a year
interpret.why: The pattern is cholestatic: ALP (about 4.7 times the upper limit of 130) and GGT are disproportionately raised compared with ALT, and bilirubin is high with dark urine and pale stools. A raised GGT shows the ALP is from the liver or bile ducts rather than bone. Ultrasound can show dilated bile ducts or gallstones. Patterns are interpreted with the clinical picture and local guidance (for example the BSG guideline).
optWhy: Correct: ALP and GGT are markedly raised relative to ALT, and imaging is the first step to look for obstruction.
ALT is only mildly raised; the dominant rise in ALP and GGT is cholestatic.
A raised GGT points to the liver, and the bilirubin of 112 shows cholestasis.
This patient is jaundiced with symptoms of obstruction and needs prompt assessment.

interpret.title: A very different liver pattern
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 29-year-old presents with malaise, nausea and jaundice over a week. How is the pattern best described? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: Gilbert's syndrome: an isolated mild rise in unconjugated bilirubin
Normal liver function, as albumin is normal
Hepatocellular: the transaminases are raised far out of proportion to ALP
interpret.why: ALT is 1240 ÷ 40 = about 31 times the upper limit, with ALP only just above the range, which is hepatocellular injury. Causes include viral hepatitis, drugs and toxins. A normal albumin does not exclude acute injury, because albumin turns over slowly.
optWhy: A raised bilirubin occurs in both patterns; cholestasis shows a disproportionate rise in ALP and GGT.
Gilbert's syndrome has normal transaminases, not values in the thousands.
Albumin has a long half-life, so it may be normal in acute injury; the transaminases show active cell damage.
Correct: ALT 1240 is about 31 times the upper limit, while ALP is only slightly raised.

interpret.title: Urine dipstick in acute kidney injury
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 55-year-old has a creatinine that has doubled over a week, with no history of vomiting or diarrhoea and no obstruction on ultrasound. Which interpretation is best? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: Pre-renal injury from dehydration, as the urine is concentrated
Haematuria and proteinuria without infection suggest glomerular disease such as nephritis, and should prompt discussion with nephrology
interpret.why: NICE NG148 recommends urine dipstick testing (including blood and protein) when AKI is suspected; with no obvious cause of AKI, haematuria with proteinuria and no infection or catheter trauma should make you think about acute nephritis (for example from vasculitis) and discuss with nephrology. A specific gravity near 1.010 suggests the tubules are not concentrating, unlike a pre-renal state.
optWhy: Leucocytes and nitrite are negative, so infection is unlikely.
The specific gravity of 1.012 is not concentrated, and dehydration does not produce 3+ blood.
Correct: this dipstick pattern points to glomerular injury rather than a pre-renal cause.
It would not explain a doubling of creatinine and significant proteinuria.

interpret.title: Observations and urine output after surgery
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A man who is 84 kg is unwell after surgery. Using the NICE NG148 urine output criterion of below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours, what is the right conclusion? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: It is not met, because 38 mL/hour is above 30 mL/hour
It is not met, because it needs to be below 0.5 mL/hour
It cannot be judged without a creatinine result
The criterion is met, as 38 ÷ 84 is 0.45 mL/kg/hour, below the threshold of 42 mL/hour
interpret.why: The threshold is 0.5 × 84 = 42 mL/hour. The measured 38 mL/hour is 38 ÷ 84 = 0.45 mL/kg/hour, below 0.5, and the output has been low for 8 hours, which is more than 6. With tachycardia, relative hypotension and a temperature, this should prompt a review of cause and volume status.
optWhy: There is no fixed figure of 30 mL/hour; the criterion is based on body weight.
The unit is mL per kilogram per hour, not mL per hour.
Urine output is an independent criterion; a creatinine result is not needed.
Correct: 0.5 × 84 = 42 mL/hour and 38 is below it.
